title: King Charles, Prince William 'furious' as Princess Diana's brother unleashes explosive claims: experts
summary: Charles Spencer's "Swan Song" reopens royal family wounds with claims about Princess Diana's funeral that have rattled Buckingham Palace insiders.
story: British broadcaster Helena Chard explains how Earl Charles Spencer’s memoir is affecting King Charles and Prince William as the palace seeks to move past the controversy.
King Charles III and Prince William are said to be furious at Charles Spencer's new book, which makes damning allegations about the monarch and reopens decades-old wounds within the royal family.

The claim was made by several royal experts who spoke to Fox News Digital after "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" was published on Tuesday. In it, Princess Diana's brother says he argued with then-Prince Charles over palace plans to have William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession.

Most notably, Spencer alleged that after Diana died at age 36 in a car crash, Charles "sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner." He wrote that Charles "went ballistic" during an argument they had over William and Harry. Spencer said Charles then hissed, "Rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough."
KING CHARLES RESPONDS TO CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT PRINCESS DIANA IN A RARE STATEMENT
Charles Spencer says King Charles III "gaslit" him in response to his claims about an alleged conversation they had following Princess Diana's death. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"What I am hearing concerning the reaction around both households is frustration and anger, but for slightly different reasons," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
"For the king, I think there is genuine anger at what amounts to an attack on his character almost 30 years after Diana's death," she explained.

"But Charles has also lived with being cast as the villain in the Diana story for decades. Unfortunately, being portrayed as the bad guy in somebody else's version of this story is not new territory for him. For Prince William, there is an additional sense of betrayal. This is his uncle, who famously stood at Diana's funeral and promised that her 'blood family' would protect William and Harry."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Swan Song" by Charles Spencer is out now. (Penguin Press)
"William now has to watch that same uncle reopen some of the most traumatic events of his childhood and hear extremely damaging allegations against his father," Schofield said.
WATCH: KING CHARLES FACES RENEWED ROYAL DRAMA OVER SPENCER MEMOIR: EXPERT

"And William isn't just Charles' son. He is the future king. The monarchy Charles Spencer is attacking is the institution William will inherit. William is also reasonably questioning how dredging up disputed private conversations from 30 years ago, attacking the current king and reigniting the ugliest chapters of the Charles and Diana story could be in his nephew's best interests."
After excerpts from the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace issued a rare, strongly worded statement.

Prince William, Prince of Wales and King Charles III walk behind Queen Elizabeth II's coffin as it is transported on a gun carriage from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Hall ahead of her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. William is heir to the British throne. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital it had no comment. A spokesperson for Kensington Palace previously told Fox News Digital the palace does not comment on books.
King Charles III and Prince William attend the Thistle Service at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, Scotland, on July 1, 2026. Earl Charles Spencer's memoir has rocked the monarchy. (Getty Images)
Spencer has stood by his account, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. He asked, "Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"
Prince Charles walking alongside his sons at Princess Diana's funeral in 1997. (JEFF J. MITCHELL/AFP via Getty Images)
Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma nearly 30 years later, The Associated Press reported.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Earl Charles Spencer's book "Swan Song" was released this week. (Getty Images)

Spencer said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, "once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths."
Author Christopher Andersen told Fox News Digital he was surprised by Spencer's allegations.

From left: Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, Prince William, the 9th Earl Charles Spencer, Prince Harry, and Prince Charles, walk behind the funeral cortège, at the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales on Sept. 6, 1997, at Westminster Abbey in London. (David Levenson/Getty Images)
"Just weeks after Diana was killed, I interviewed hundreds of sources in London and Paris for my book 'The Day Diana Died,'" he said.
"The Day Diana Died" was written by Christopher Andersen. (William Morrow)

"They all remembered that Charles was absolutely devastated. 'Crushed' was a word I heard repeatedly when he first learned the news of Diana's death. After years of famously battling as a married couple, they had finally found a kind of peace with each other following their 1996 divorce. They actually became friends."

"When Charles got the call at Balmoral that Diana had been killed, a staffer told me that the king let out a howl that sounded like a wounded animal, then burst into tears. Others described Charles at the time as being racked with sobs, his face streaked with tears."
Undated family file picture of Lady Diana Spencer (Diana, Princess of Wales) with her Brother Charles, Lord Alhorp (Earl Spencer) in 1968. (PA Images via Getty Images)
"I also interviewed the nurses at the Paris hospital who witnessed the moment Charles saw Diana's body for the first time," Andersen continued.

"He fell back, one of them told me, as if he had been struck by an unseen hand. They thought he was going to pass out. He then began to weep openly. Everyone was very surprised at how emotional King Charles was because they believed members of the royal family, and especially Charles, were cold and aloof. They did not doubt in their minds that he was shattered by his ex-wife's tragic death."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
A multicolored sea of floral tributes lies outside the gates of Princess Diana's London home after news of her death in a Paris car crash reached Britain. (Liba Taylor/Corbis)
Andersen said he wonders whether the words Spencer says he heard from Charles over the phone were those of "a man on the verge of a nervous breakdown."

"King Charles' world was crumbling all around him," Andersen said. "Not only was the mother of his children suddenly gone, but at the time, Queen Elizabeth did not want the princess to have a public funeral. She refused to fly the flag at half-staff over Buckingham Palace in Diana's honor. She did not even want to come back from her summer vacation at Balmoral. It fell on Charles' shoulders to force his mother to show Diana the respect the British people felt she deserved."

Prince Charles kisses Lady Sarah McCorquodale as Lady Jane Fellowes looks on at RAF Northolt Airport near London on Aug. 31, 1997, following the arrival of the casket containing the body of Diana, Princess of Wales. (AFP via Getty Images)
Still, Andersen said he would not be surprised if the king had shouted hurtful words at Spencer in anger.
An aerial view shows the burial site of Diana, Princess of Wales, at the Althorp Estate in Althorp, United Kingdom. (David Goddard/Getty Images)
"Charles has a long history of lashing out, making rash and sometimes cruel, offhand statements," Andersen said.

"The king always resented being overshadowed by Diana during her lifetime, and now he was being totally eclipsed by her in death. There was lingering resentment there. It's also clear the king knew that the public would blame him and Camilla for making Diana so desperately unhappy during her lifetime and, to some extent, for the extent, for the events leading up to her death."
At Princess Diana's funeral, Queen Elizabeth II greets mourners waiting in line to sign the condolence book. (Corbis via Getty Images)

Andersen noted that the late queen "was in no mood" to see her eldest son remarry anytime soon. Any hopes Charles may have had of marrying Camilla, with whom he had previously had an affair, were dashed. Eight years passed before the queen permitted Charles to marry Camilla.
A source told Radar Online that Queen Camilla is trying to "lower the temperature" behind palace doors.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

"She doesn't believe anything is gained by continually reopening old wounds or allowing deeply personal disagreements about the past to develop into an increasingly hostile public battle," the insider told the outlet.

"Camilla is particularly conscious that there are different memories of what happened during an extraordinarily difficult period for the family. People experienced those events from very different perspectives, and she recognizes that emotions surrounding Diana are still exceptionally powerful."
Lady Diana Spencer and Camilla Parker-Bowles attend the Ludlow Races where Prince Charles is competing, circa 1980. (Express Newspapers/Archive Photos)
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that William isn't close to his uncle and that sources have told her he is "absolutely furious."

Britain's Princess Anne, Princess Royal, and Britain's Prince William, Prince of Wales, leave after the funeral service for the late King Harald V of Norway before the casket is moved in a procession from Oslo Cathedral to Akershus Castle in Oslo, Norway, on Sept. 9, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
"His public silence regarding this matter is admirable," she said. "The pain Spencer is causing William has backfired as he’s being accused of monetizing his sister’s memory."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that Buckingham Palace is "rattled, but they're not panicking" over Spencer's "verbal grenades straight at the palace gates." She said the royal family is privately presenting a united front as its members focus on their duties.
A general view of Buckingham Palace in London, England, on July 6, 2026. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

"The strategy is clear: let the book have a few weeks of noisy publicity and just plow on with the job," Chard said. "Sources say King Charles is saddened, yet angry, and sort of feels like a lamb to the slaughter facing never-ending character assassination. For Prince William, the pain cuts slightly deeper. It's trauma stirred anew. Palace aides say his focus is on public work and protecting the family."
PRINCESS DIANA'S BROTHER CHARLES SPENCER SAYS KING CHARLES 'GASLIT' HIM OVER MEMOIR CLAIMS
Spencer found it "bizarre and cruel" to make Prince William and Prince Harry walk behind their mother's coffin at her funeral. (Jeff Overs/BBC News & Current Affairs via Getty Images)
"Whatever you think of Prince Harry's memoir, Harry was King Charles' son, Prince William's brother and a central participant in the family life he was describing," Schofield said.
Prince Charles and Princess Diana's divorce was finalized in 1996. (Anwar Hussein/Getty Images)

"Charles Spencer simply did not have that same proximity to the royal family or even, according to multiple accounts, to Diana throughout the final years of her life. There have been people within Diana's circle who have challenged the impression that Charles Spencer was this constant, intimate presence in her life."
Spencer has stood by his account as the book rolls out globally and is translated into 12 languages.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Madonna dominates VMAs with Artist of the Year win after showstopping opening performance
summary: Madonna commanded attention at the MTV VMAs, winning seven awards and opening the show with star-studded performance.
story: Former MTV executive Van Toffler discusses Madonna and Nirvana ahead of the 2026 VMAs, airing live Sept. 27 at 7:30 PM ET on CBS and MTV, streaming on Paramount+ Premium and returning to Los Angeles since 2017.
Madonna took home a number of awards at the 2026 MTV VMAs, including the biggest honor of the night, Artist of the Year.
She also won Best Collaboration and Best Dance awards, bringing her total 2026 VMAs award wins to seven.
During the show, which was hosted by Snoop Dogg at Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Kacey Musgraves channeled Dolly Parton in a tribute to the late country icon.
She sang Parton's song, "I Will Always Love You" for her tribute, one month after Parton's death.
Taylor Swift won Video of the Year for her music video "The Fate of Ophelia." Swift wrote and directed the music video for her song. Swift dedicated her win to Parton.
She also received the first ever Artist Director Honors, presented by her friend Dakota Johnson. Swift also received the award for Best Direction for "Opalite."
Madonna won a total of seven MTV VMAs. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for The Met Museum/Vogue)
Madonna opened the show with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX — 23 years after her last performance for the ceremony.
She performed "Bring Your Love" with Sabrina Carpenter, and "Danceteria" with Charli XCX.
There were also guest appearances by Julia Garner, Sombr, Debi Mazar and Seth Rogen in her show-opener performance.
Madonna pictured at the VMAs on Sunday night with Taylor Swift. (Christopher Polk/CBS via Getty Images)
Fans took to X to share their reaction to Madonna’s performance.
"Train wreck," one fan wrote, adding that she "looked like she was hanging on for dear life."
Another called her performance "cringeworthy," and someone else wrote on X: "Much of her performance was just embarrassing… lip-sync & awkward moves....still happy for her wins btw."
Others gushed about her performance. One fan wrote: "I’m proud of Madonna. That was a great performance & great showcase of the creative vision of the album. THEE QUEEN."
Others said: "Can’t get enough," "Insane performance," "killed it tonight," "What a great performance thank u Mother Madonna u continue to amaze me."
Madonna beat Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Sabrina Carpenter, Bruno Mars and Morgan Wallen for the Artist of the Year.
The artist began her acceptance speech by thanking her fingers "because I can always count on them."
Madonna also pointed out that the audience wasn’t born when she performed at the first ever MTV Video Music Awards, which took place in 1984. She had sung "Like A Virgin."
Taylor Swift accepted the Video of the Year Award for "The Fate of Ophelia" onstage at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. (Rich Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)
She said during her performance her shoe fell off, calling it a "little problem."
Madonna recalled she tried to dive and grab her shoe by trying to make herself "look cute and sexy."
"I had a little problem with my shoes and I dove onto the stage to try and make myself look cute and sexy and like I meant to do it."
However, she said by doing so, she accidentally flashed her backside.

The singer said in the last year and a half, she focused on "finding myself, believing in myself, and really making the music that I wanted to make."

She added: "I mean, that really is the definition of being an artist. And my hope for all of you here tonight is that you spend the next year, or the next 10 years, or put the rest of your life doing the same, finding yourself and believing in yourself."

title: 'Home Improvement' star says Patricia Richardson got 'tired' of fighting for sitcom
summary: Taran Noah Smith reveals Patricia Richardson fought to keep "Home Improvement" realistic as new writers pushed scripts in a different direction.
story: Patricia Richardson explained to Fox News Digital that Tim Allen was better on "Home Improvement" than many of the seasoned actors she had worked with before.
"Home Improvement" star Taran Noah Smith is shedding new light on why the hit 1990s sitcom came to an end.

The 42-year-old former actor was seven-years-old when he landed the role of Mark Taylor, the youngest son of Tim "The Tool Man" Taylor (Tim Allen) and his wife Jill Taylor (Patricia Richardson) in 1991.

The sitcom, which was based on Allen's stand-up comedy persona, centered on Tim, a television host known for his home improvement show, "Tool Time," and his family life with Jill, Mark and older sons Brad (Zachery Ty Bryan) and Randy (Jonathan Taylor Thomas).
"Home Improvement" star Taran Noah Smith opened up about why the hit sitcom came to an end. (Patricia Richardson Instagram/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
'HOME IMPROVEMENT' STAR JONATHAN TAYLOR THOMAS ARRESTED FOR ALLEGED PUBLIC INTOXICATION, RESISTING DEPUTY

"Home Improvement" became one of the highest-rated shows of the '90s and ran for eight seasons and aired 204 episodes. However, the show concluded in 1999 after Richardson declined to return for a proposed ninth season.

During a recent appearance on Tom Scharpling and Julia Vickerman's podcast "Outgrown" podcast, Smith reflected on his time starring on the show and weighed in on the reasons behind Richardson's departure.
TIM ALLEN SAYS HE 'NEVER REALLY WANTED' TO BE A DAD AND OPENS UP ABOUT SOBRIETY AND FATHERHOOD REGRETS
Smith recalled that Richardson joined the cast as Jill just days before the pilot was taped after producers replaced Frances Fisher, the actress originally cast as Tim's wife, during rehearsals.
"Home Improvement" was one of the highes-rated shows of the 1990s and ran for eight seasons from 1991 to 1998.  (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"When they brought Patricia in, there was just a much better chemistry," he said. "And she had her own kid. She had just given birth to twins, and she had one older kid who was about my age. She really brought a lot more of a realistic mom energy to her, and she fought throughout the whole show to keep the show more realistic."
"She would tell the writers, ‘A mother would never say this,’ and get them to change it," he added.
Smith said he "definitely" agreed with Richardson's input though he acknowledged that he and the show's other child stars weren't really involved in conversations about the script.
"They'd do a run-through of the script on Monday and then the kids would go to school usually, and they would continue to discuss the script," he said.
Smith recalled that there were creative disagreements on set after a new creative team replaced the show's original writers and producers.
ROSEANNE BARR HASN’T SPOKEN TO TV SISTER LAURIE METCALF SINCE SHOW’S CANCELLATION

The show followed TV host Tim "The Tool Man" Taylor (Tim Allen) and his family life with wife Jill Taylor (Patricia Richardson) and sons Brad (Zachery Ty Bryan), Randy (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) and Mark (Taran Noah Smith).  (Getty)

"The original creators only did the first couple seasons, and then they moved on, and they brought in a whole other group of writer/producers," he remembered. "Those guys, very few of them had kids, and the show kind of started to go in a different direction, at least the scripts we'd get on Monday."

"It was really Pat, the mom, who fought the good fight to make it more realistic because oftentimes it would just be something that was very out of character just to sell a joke, just to set up a joke," he continued. "It's like, ‘Wait, this is not what the characters are about.’"
ROSEANNE BARR CALLS FORMER CO-STAR A 'BRAINWASHED BIGOT' AFTER HE SAID REBOOT WAS 'RIGHTFULLY CANCELED'

Smith speculated that Allen was reluctant to appear overly controlling after witnessing what happened on another sitcom, "Roseanne." "Roseanne," which became an instant hit after it premiered in 1988, was created by "Home Improvement" co-creator Matt Williams. Like "Home Improvement," Roseanne was built around its star's stand-up comedy voice and persona.

However, Barr clashed behind-the-scenes with producers and writers, including Williams, over the direction and tone of the show. The tensions between the two led to Williams leaving after the first season. Barr later gained more influence and was credited as a creator in later seasons.
Patricia Richardson starred opposite Tim Allen in "Home Improvement," but would not be interested in doing a reboot. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
‘THE OFFICE’ STAR JENNA FISCHER EXPOSES THE GRUELING REALITY THAT FORCED HER OFF TV

"I think Tim was overall maybe a bit worried about being a tyrant because the same creators created ‘Roseanne,’ and Roseanne took over the show and fired the creators, fired everybody," Smith recalled. "Actually, all our camera crew had been fired in one day from ‘Roseanne’ and came over to us. So, Tim was always, I think, more hands-off with that, not wanting to be tyrannical, which meant that it was a lot more on Pat to push."
"That's one of the reasons why the show ended up eventually ending, because she was just tired of it, of having to fight to make it realistic all the time," he continued.
JODIE SWEETIN SHARES SHOCKING 'FULL HOUSE' RESIDUAL CHECK AMOUNT DESPITE SHOW'S MEGA SUCCESS

"And Tim was getting far more money than she was," Smith added. "That was her actual way of stopping. She said she'd do a ninth season if she got paid the same amount as Tim, knowing they wouldn't do it."
Smith's recollection of why Richardson left "Home Improvement" echoes what the actress has said for years about her experience on the show and the reasons for her departure.
During a May 2024 interview with the Los Angeles Times, Richardson recalled that the creators emphasized the importance of the character of Jill and her relationship with Tim.

Smith said that Allen took a more "hands-off" approach to creative disagreements with directors and writers, leaving Richardson to fight for character consistency.  ( ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
"When I took the job, they said it wasn’t meant to be the Tim Allen show. It was meant to be our show," she said. "I’ve always said, I don’t want to play the thankless wife."

Richardson recalled having creative disagreements with male writers over how Jill would react to specific situations, remembering one instance in which she was told, "Pat, it’s not like we don’t understand women. We’re married to them."
The actress, who earned four Primetime Emmy Award nominations for her performance as Jill, told the LA Times that she made the decision to leave the show.

Richardson told the LA Times she decided during the eighth season that it would be her last, citing a desire to spend more time with her children after her divorce and her belief that the sitcom had run its course, pointing to Jonathan Taylor Thomas' departure and declining ratings.

Smith said that Richardson left the show after growing "tired" of fighting to make the show realistic.  (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

The actress also felt that Disney failed to recognize her creative contributions to the series, saying she helped shape her character and storylines but was denied a producer credit, even as Allen became an executive producer.
"I told everybody, there’s not enough money in the world to get me to do a ninth year. This show is over. It needs to end," Richardson recalled.

Richardson recalled that ABC unexpectedly offered to continue the show with a 25-episode ninth season. She said the network's parent company, Disney, proposed paying her a salary of $1 million an episode, while Allen would be paid $2 million an episode.

Though she recalled Allen immediately accepting the offer, she said she countered with terms that she knew the studio would reject. Richardson told the outlet that she requested equal pay with Allen and an executive producer credit.

"I knew that Disney would in no way pay me that much. That was my way to say ‘no’ and was a little bit of a flip-off to Disney," Richardson said. "I’d been there all this time, and they never even paid me a third of what Tim was making, and I was working my a-- off. I was a big reason why women were watching."

title: Rapid weight loss on popular drugs could ‘starve’ the brain, expert warns
summary: Dr. Tommy Wood warns GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy can shrink brain tissue when caloric restriction cuts off vital energy the brain needs.
story: Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, shares how GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic can affect brain reserve, and why resistance training is critical to protect it.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said the drugs' effects on the brain may depend on whether the body is getting enough energy and nutrients during weight loss.

"The best way to think about this is the spectrum of what we call energy availability," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong NY, New York City's largest annual fitness and wellness festival. "The brain is your most energy-hungry organ in the body."
POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER
According to Wood, brain reserve — the physical amount and integrity of brain tissue — follows a bell-shaped curve relative to the body's energy availability.
Excess energy caused by obesity, high blood sugar and metabolic disease can lower the brain's resilience by damaging blood vessels and contributing to insulin resistance.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients. (iStock)
In these cases, GLP-1 medications can provide cognitive benefits by lowering blood pressure and improving blood sugar control.

However, Wood noted that the lower end of the energy spectrum poses its own structural risks to the brain. Because the brain relies heavily on continuous fuel, extreme caloric deficits can force the organ to consume its own tissue.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS CAN BECOME AN ‘ATOMIC BOMB’ AT HIGH DOSES, DOCTOR WARNS

"There was a study that looked at the brains of people who ran a marathon ... because the marathon is so energy-intensive, the white matter in the brain actually shrank during a marathon because the brain didn't have enough energy … so it was eating its own white matter," Wood said, noting that the participants' brains recovered after resting and refueling.
"It just shows that the brain is really energy-hungry, and it will decrease its size if it's not getting enough energy."
If people aren't eating enough, they're not getting the nutrients that are critical for brain health, according to Wood. (iStock)
Muscle quality
Concerns about lean muscle loss when taking GLP-1 medications are often nuanced, Wood said. Some of the early "lean mass" that's lost is actually fat that had built up inside the muscles.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"So technically, your muscles get smaller, but you don't get weaker," he told Fox News Digital. "And the quality and functioning of your muscles actually gets better."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

However, risks arise when individuals taking GLP-1 medications drastically reduce their food intake for extended periods. Chronic under-eating can deprive the central nervous system of essential structural nutrients, Wood warned.
Ensuring adequate intake of core neuro-nutrients — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment. (iStock)

"It is possible that you can end up going too far," he said. "If you're not eating enough, you're not getting the nutrients that are critical for the brain. So you're not getting in enough omega-3 fats, which we know are really important. You're not getting enough iron and protein and all those kinds of things."
Protecting the brain during weight loss

To safeguard brain health while losing weight, Wood recommends pairing weight-loss regimens with resistance training twice a week to maintain functional muscle mass and to stimulate brain growth factors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, ensuring adequate intake of core "neuro-nutrients" — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment, according to Wood.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For most people, I think it's going to be beneficial to start, but you just need to make sure that you don't push it too far, that you're now getting enough of everything that the brain needs," he advised.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Heavy drinking surges among Americans in one age group as other generations cut back
summary: Adults ages 50 to 64 saw heavy drinking surge more than 36% since 2018, even as overall U.S. alcohol use finally began to decline post-pandemic.
story: Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, discusses why alcohol poses higher risks to people as they age, and shares tips for moderating intake.

New research shows that U.S. alcohol use has declined for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, but drinking remains above pre-pandemic levels — with one particular group showing a sharp increase in heavy intake.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%.
Across all age groups, alcohol use declined by nearly 2%, and heavy drinking declined by more than 8% from 2022 to 2024. However, overall alcohol use remained above pre-pandemic levels.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
Among Gen Z adults, alcohol use declined by more than 5%. Millennials drank approximately 17% less from 2022 to 2024.

The findings, which were published on Sept. 21 in Annals of Internal Medicine, were based on self-reported data from the National Health Interview Survey, which included 114,352 U.S. adults from 2018 to 2024.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%. (iStock)
Heavy drinking was defined as five or more drinks per day or 15 or more drinks per week for men within the preceding 12 months and at least four daily drinks or eight weekly drinks for women.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%).
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

"Women’s heavy drinking rose more than men's during the pandemic and is still about 13% above where it was in 2018," lead study author Brian P. Lee, M.D., associate professor of medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, told Fox News Digital. "Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
The study was funded in part by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism and the National Institutes of Health.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%). (iStock)
Study limitations
The chief limitation of the study is that people reported their own levels of drinking, which tend to run low, according to Lee.

"It also can't tell us why drinking changed, only that it did," he told Fox News Digital. "And we have two years of decline after four years of increases, so I'd describe this as a promising turn rather than an established trend."
The researchers also did not investigate the reasons younger adults reduced alcohol consumption.
"Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
Potential reasons older adults are drinking more
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, said many factors may contribute to the increased rate of drinking among older adults.
"As we approach our 50s and 60s, we start reflecting on our lives, and changes start to happen," Tuell, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to an addiction expert. (iStock)
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to Tuell.
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members.

"One out of four people will experience some mental health issue … depression, anxiety, loss, grief — these are real things that are impacting people," Tuell said. "And it's at a time where a person might feel very vulnerable."
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
As people age, there may also be increased issues related to chronic pain and medical issues, resulting in reduced function.
"Now I have these aches and pains, or maybe I'm diagnosed with something more serious," Tuell said as an example. "So that becomes a problem that I now have to deal with."
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members. (iStock)
Many aging adults are also approaching retirement age, which can result in a loss of structure and change the identity they’ve had for decades, the expert noted.

"I wake up and something I've done every day for many, many years is no longer happening. So I'm more bored. What do I do with my time? This is unfortunately a perfect storm for things like substance use."
Risks of alcohol for older adults
As older adults experience body changes, they don't metabolize alcohol the same way they once did, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What I used to drink maybe five years ago … that same amount now can affect me differently, because I'm not metabolizing it like I used to," he said.
Women are especially impacted by alcohol, Tuell said, likely because they may have less body fat and don't have as much water in their bodies.
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, the lead researcher recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong." (iStock)
Lee noted that while alcohol doesn't harm everyone equally, the risk starts at low levels and goes up with every additional drink.
"There isn't a level the evidence shows to be safe."
Red flags
To determine whether someone has a problem with alcohol, Tuell recommends using the "three Cs."

Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."Can’t: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."

Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."
Can’t: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Alcohol can still be problematic even if someone doesn’t have an addiction, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For example, they might drink more than they should, to the point where they get a hangover or put themselves at risk.
"Maybe it's impacting my interactions with other people, interpersonal relationships, hobbies, interests," he said. "Maybe it's affecting my sleep."
In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, the expert said. (iStock)

In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, Tuell said. "So, we're not getting good rest during that period."
It’s never too late to seek help with alcohol dependency, he pointed out.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I've treated people in their 80s who still have a lot of life left," Tuell said, pointing out that Americans are living longer. "So we're aging, we're getting older, and there are a lot of life changes happening … physically, emotionally, psychologically."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, Lee recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong."

"There are clear increases in cancer and liver risk with alcohol, even at low levels," he warned. "Even advanced liver disease might have no symptoms, and the earlier alcohol-related liver damage is caught, the more of it can be undone."

title: Dengue fever outbreak triggers states of emergency in 3 southern counties
summary: Three Florida counties declared emergencies as 190 locally acquired dengue fever cases were confirmed, with Hillsborough County reporting 170 infections.
story: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Professor Dr. Marty Makary weighs in on whether Americans should be concerned about the rise in both COVID cases and Dengue fever in the U.S. and discusses Potassium Chloride meds being recalled for heart risks.
Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state.
As of Sept. 23, Pasco County, Hillsborough County and Pinellas County have made the declarations due to a spread of the mosquito-borne disease, according to each county’s news release.

The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement, the releases state.
TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE
Under Florida law, local emergency declarations expire after seven days unless they are renewed.

A total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases have been confirmed across six Florida counties, according to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report, which covered cases with onset through Sept. 19.
Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state. (Getty Images)
Of the 190 locally acquired cases, 170 were reported in Hillsborough County, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties, three in Orange County, two in Pasco County and one in Palm Beach County.
The 190 locally acquired infections are separate from travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year.
TICK-BORNE 'RABBIT FEVER' SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida."

Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital.

"As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important," the expert went on. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk."
Stopping the spread

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports.

The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement. (iStock)

FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health entomologist shared the following recommendations to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne disease.

Use an EPA-registered insect repellent: Review, follow and apply repellent label directions to help prevent mosquito bites.Eliminate sources of standing water nearby: Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites.Layer repellent and sunscreen correctly: When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed.Protect throughout the day: Don’t limit mosquito precautions to dawn and dusk. The Aedes mosquitoes that can spread dengue are active throughout the day, so use protection whenever mosquito exposure is possible.
Use an EPA-registered insect repellent: Review, follow and apply repellent label directions to help prevent mosquito bites.

Eliminate sources of standing water nearby: Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites.

Layer repellent and sunscreen correctly: When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed.

Protect throughout the day: Don’t limit mosquito precautions to dawn and dusk. The Aedes mosquitoes that can spread dengue are active throughout the day, so use protection whenever mosquito exposure is possible.
The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.
Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. (iStock)
Symptoms and treatment
Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.
Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito.

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness.
People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

title: ‘Superman’ star Christopher Reeve’s son reveals 'shock' cancer diagnosis at age 34
summary: Will Reeve, son of Christopher Reeve, revealed his embryonal carcinoma diagnosis and orchiectomy on air, drawing parallels to his parents' battles.
story: "Super/Man: The Christopher Reeve Story" co-director Peter Ettedgui told Fox News Digital that Reeve’s wife, children and friend Robin Williams made the actor realize he wanted to live after becoming paralyzed.
Will Reeve, son of the late famed "Superman" actor Christopher Reeve, announced that he recently battled cancer.
The "Good Morning America" correspondent, 34, shared during Tuesday’s show that he was diagnosed with testicular cancer earlier this year, assuring viewers that he is "OK."

"The diagnosis was a shock and the treatments were a slog," he said. "Today, though, I am relieved to announce that we arrived at our destination and this cancer is in the rearview mirror. But what a journey."
WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS DOCTOR DISMISSED KEY WARNING SIGN BEFORE STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS
Reeve said he found a "hard, tender lump in [his] left testicle" just a few months after his wedding to luxury event planner Amanda Dubin.
Will Reeve (left), son of the late famed "Superman" star Christopher Reeve (right), announced he recently battled cancer. (Getty Images)
An ultrasound revealed that he had "a mass that had to come out." After undergoing surgery to remove the testicle (an orchiectomy), Reeve discovered the mass was embryonal carcinoma.
The aggressive subtype of testicular cancer can spread more quickly than some other forms, according to the American Cancer Society.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES
Reeve later underwent a second surgery to remove lymph nodes from his abdomen after some cancer cells had spread there.
The surgery took place at Memorial Sloan Kettering, which is where his mother, Dana Reeve, died from lung cancer in 2006 at age 44. His father died in 2004 at the age of 52.
Actor Robin Williams, right, poses with actor Christopher Reeve, wife Dana Reeve and son Will, left, at the 2004 Tribeca Film Festival in May 2004. (Evan Agostini/Getty Images)

Reeve shared that he also underwent two rounds of chemotherapy to lower the risk that the cancer would return. He said he experienced several side effects from the medication, including ringing in the ears, bone pain, night sweats, blood clots and constant headaches.

He did not lose his hair because he used a method called "cold capping," which is used during certain chemotherapy treatments to help reduce hair loss by cooling the scalp and constricting blood vessels.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
After finishing his second round of chemotherapy on July 31, Reeve said he received "clean scans" on Sept. 8.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In an interview with People, Reeve said he is "going to be fine," although it has been "one heck of a chapter."

"I’m fortunate that I caught this early," he said. "Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor."

Actor Christopher Reeve gets a kiss from his son Will during a "20/20" special interview Sept. 29, 1995, in New Jersey. The show was Reeve's first appearance since his horseback riding accident. (Getty Images)
Reeve also praised his wife for serving as his "caregiver," similar to how his mother helped care for his father after a 1995 horseback-riding accident left him paralyzed.
"I learn[ed] more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him," Reeve said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
He added that the experience taught him how to "repurpose [adversity] into something hopeful."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Testicular cancer is among the most treatable cancers, particularly when detected early, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts recommend seeing a doctor promptly for any lump, swelling, pain or change in a testicle.

title: 4 simple habits can help slow muscle loss as you age, fitness expert says
summary: A fitness coach reveals four key strategies to slow age-related muscle loss, from daily protein intake to strength training and sleep habits.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.

As Americans increasingly turn to GLP-1 medications — which have been linked to a loss of lean muscle, especially during rapid weight loss — experts say preserving strength and mobility should be a priority as people age.

Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said that beyond GLP-1s, there are several other reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.
"The biggest change is lifestyle," he told Fox News Digital. "When you're in your teen years or your 20s, you're running around, you're doing activities that lend themselves to building muscle."
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
That tends to change as people shift focus to career and family, the expert said.
"You simply become more sedentary, which lowers your metabolism and your level of activity, so you're going to have less muscle."
The expert said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age. (iStock)
As people approach their 40s, hormone levels begin to change for both men and women, Zemer noted.
"That means we partition the calories we're using less and less for protein and building muscle, and more and more for simply storing as fat," he said.
THIS EXERCISE HABIT MAY SLASH DEMENTIA RISK AND HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY FINDS
"We see this all the time … people start to store fat in their tummies, and they start have less muscle."
Zemer said he believes that everyone should be "very mindful" about building muscle, starting from a young age.

For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms). (iStock)
"All the way up into your 50s, your goal should be to build muscle so that when you enter your golden years — your 60s, 70s, 80s — it's kind of like your 401K," he said.

"You're going to be depleting from it as you go through life. So in your 30s and 40s, you just have to be more strategic about it, because your lifestyle has changed. You need to go to the gym and train in order to have that muscle later in life."
Zemer shared the following strategies that can help people slow down muscle loss as they age.
No. 1: Get adequate protein
Protein helps to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, the body's process of repairing and building muscle, according to Zemer.
EATING TOO MUCH PROTEIN COULD BACKFIRE, EXPERTS WARN AFTER LONGEVITY REVIEW
Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, which is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength.
While people’s protein needs will vary based on age, activity level and fitness goals, Zemer said people who regularly strength-train generally benefit from higher intake.
Including enough protein in your daily diet can help reduce the risk of sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. (iStock)

"If you're a sedentary person, you don't need to be obsessed with protein," he told Fox News Digital. "Very few people aren't getting enough protein in terms of macronutrients. But if you're training and going to the gym, you want to be getting somewhere between 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight."
No. 2: Strength-train regularly

For general health, the U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend that adults strength train at least two days per week, working all major muscle groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms).
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises using moderate or greater intensity until it's difficult to complete another repetition with good form.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The guidelines also recommend pairing the strength training with 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity) each week.
Lifting weights isn’t just about building muscle, but also preserving muscle, according to Zemer.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Even if you have a busy week, and you went to the gym and you lifted weights 30 minutes twice a week, that may not be enough to build new muscle, but that is certainly enough to maintain muscle," he said.
"So it's very important that you lift weights a couple of times a week as you age."
For beginners, the trainer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. (iStock)

For beginners, Zemer recommends focusing on a few basic functional movements. Body-weight exercises like squats, lunges, push-ups and pulling movements help build strength for everyday activities, while carrying weighted objects — known as a farmer's carry, Zemer said — can improve grip, balance and overall stability.
For people who feel intimidated by the gym, working with a qualified trainer for a few sessions can help boost confidence and refine technique, according to Zemer.
No. 3: Get sufficient sleep
Perhaps the most difficult strategy for maintaining muscle is to get enough quality sleep — seven to nine hours, Zemer emphasized.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Now, if you don't get that every night, you're not going to lose muscle," he noted. "But when you start to look at actual serious sleep deficiency, like we're talking five hours consistently, that is when you see rapid muscle loss."
No. 4: Find alternatives if necessary
"The worst thing you can do, even if you're injured, is to stop doing anything," Zemer said.

Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned. (iStock)
"Find things you can do. Even if something hurts you, even if your knees aren't like what they used to be."
Even without structured workouts, regular movement can help slow age-related muscle loss, while being sedentary is associated with rapid declines in muscle mass and strength, the expert cautioned.
GLP-1s and muscle loss

The above strategies are especially important for people who are taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, Zemer noted, as these drugs can lead to muscle loss in the absence of strength training or adequate protein.

"If you are on a GLP-1, just remember you're accelerating the rate of fat loss, but you're also accelerating the rate of lean muscle," he said.
"You want to make sure you're getting that protein and training, so that you are not losing muscle on top of the fat loss."

title: Sylvester Stallone reveals surprising health struggle behind his famously ripped physique
summary: Sylvester Stallone revealed he became bulimic while prepping for "Rambo" and reached 2.6% body fat during "Rocky III" in a stunning new interview.
story: Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist in Summit, New Jersey, said it was "incredibly admirable" for Stallone to share his experience.
Sylvester Stallone is sharing some health obstacles he has faced while playing physically demanding roles over the decades.
The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he has suffered from an eating disorder.

While prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo," Stallone — who has authored a new memoir, titled "The Steps" — said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats.
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER
"Then it became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview.
Actor Sylvester Stallone, as Rocky Balboa, shows off his muscles in the boxing ring on the set of Rocky III in May 1982 in Los Angeles, California. (James Drake/Getty Images)

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).

"I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing," Stallone shared.
CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER CLAVICULAR EXPLAINS VIRAL 'LOOKSMAXXING' TREND AS GEN Z ADOPTS EXTREME REGIMEN

The actor said that while filming "Rocky III," he reached his lowest body fat of 2.6%. The National Academy of Sports Medicine classifies body fat as "dangerously low" if it falls below 8% for men ages 20–69 and below 14% for women ages 20–69.

Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith, watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the film, "Rocky," directed by John G. Avildsen, 1976. (Getty Images)
Stallone also admitted that he took steroids during some time periods. "You have to," he said. "But you do it in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off … that also took a terrible toll."

Years of injuries sustained while doing his own stunts — something he described as "very masochistic" — have also taken a toll on Stallone’s body, he said, leading to multiple surgeries on his back, shoulder and neck.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I’ve abused my body," he said. "Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape."
Stallone also revealed that he has dealt with anxiety over the decades, recounting the first incident while watching footage from one of his films when he was 36 years old.
"I’ve abused my body," Stallone said in the New York Times interview. "Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape." (Getty Images)
"All of a sudden, I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, ‘I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out,’" he said in the interview.

The actor said the panic attacks happened "again and again and again," often resurfacing before high-profile television appearances. As he aged, Stallone continued to experience anxiety and sometimes felt compelled to leave crowded rooms.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, said it was "incredibly admirable" for Stallone to share his experience.

"There are so many examples of what can take place in Sylvester Stallone's life that have led him to moments of objectivity and body awareness," Pollack, who has not treated Stallone, told Fox News Digital.
Rocky Balboa (Sylvester Stallone) skips rope under the watchful eye of his manager, Mickey (Burgess Meredith), and trainer Johnny (Stuart K. Robinson) in Rocky II. (Getty Images)

The expert suggested that a desire to maintain his success may have fueled Stallone’s rigid routines, steroid use, intense performance expectations, fear of failure, and the pressures associated with the entertainment industry.
"The idea that a man enhances his appearance to remain consistent with his own public image and internal comfort goes back decades — [Stallone] isn’t the first, and he isn’t the last," Pollack said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"He has to almost keep himself in this homeostatic state where people expect Sylvestor Stallone to be Rocky, which is his quintessential role," he went on.

"And through his career, one could surmise the need to be able to put all of that together and keep it consistent as he goes through the development and life cycles of maturation, not only in his brain, but also in his body."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Giulia Suro, a licensed clinical psychologist and certified eating disorder expert at Monte Nido in Washington, D.C., added that the Sylvester Stallone revelation was a "game-changer."
"Eating disorders continue to be misconstrued as primarily female illnesses," she told Fox News Digital.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs can become an ‘atomic bomb’ at high doses, doctor warns
summary: Dr. Will Cole warns that macro-dosing GLP-1s isn't the answer to metabolic health, advocating for micro-dosing peptides paired with lifestyle changes.
story: Dr. Will Cole discusses peptide therapy, arguing that medications affecting appetite should be used carefully alongside nutrition, exercise and other lifestyle interventions.
As interest in peptides continues to grow, experts are increasingly looking beyond weight loss to their potential role in healthy aging.
Functional medicine expert Dr. Will Cole told Fox News Digital that peptides are "intimately connected" with longevity, cellular healing and metabolic health.

"[Peptides] help with cellular communication," said Cole, co-author of the upcoming book "Heal Your Cells." The recommendations for peptides depend on the context in which they're used, he said, noting that the answer often falls "somewhere in the middle."
THINKING ABOUT PEPTIDES? DOCTORS REVEAL KEY DOS AND DON’TS AS ‘WILD WEST’ MARKET GROWS

Citing previous research, Cole noted that an estimated 93% of U.S. adults are metabolically unhealthy, leaving only about 7% who meet the criteria for optimal metabolic health — a figure he described as "wild."
Peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair. (iStock)
"That's common, but not normal," Cole said. He added that while GLP-1 medications can be beneficial, improving metabolic health also requires addressing lifestyle and other underlying factors.
FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY
Cole shared that he does not believe "macro-dosing" GLP-1s "forever and ever in perpetuity" is the solution to improving metabolic health.

While GLP-1s can reduce food cravings — often referred to as "food noise" — and promote weight loss, Cole said he’d like to see more research on how decreasing the desire for food could also decrease cravings for love, relationships and other mood-boosting factors.

The semaglutide weight-loss drug Wegovy, made by pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, is designed to treat type 2 diabetes, but is widely known for its weight-loss effect. (James Manning/PA Images via Getty Images)
Cole questioned whether suppressing food cravings could have unintended effects on other reward-related behaviors, including social relationships.
"So, are we circumventing pathways and pathologizing things that don't have to be pathologized?"
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Cole argued that some degree of hunger signaling is healthy. "Food noise is actually a decent thing in balance, so shutting down your hunger cues with an 'atomic bomb' peptide dose is not the solution."
He added that he believes overreliance on GLP-1 medications may contribute to disordered eating patterns and a growing fear of hunger.
The expert said he believes that overreliance on GLP-1 medications may contribute to disordered eating patterns and a growing fear of hunger. (iStock)
Cole attributed the trend to a culture that favors simple, fast solutions over sustained lifestyle changes. "We want a magic pill," he said.
"And the truth is somewhere in the middle: Can we micro-dose? Can we do it cyclically? And can we pair it with lifestyle?"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The expert questioned why there has been an "epidemic rise" of metabolic problems, pointing to factors such as diets high in ultraprocessed foods, nutrient deficiencies, environmental toxins and the presence of stress and trauma.
"That is why we're seeing a rise of chronic health problems, not a pharmaceutical deficiency," he said.
Pairing peptides with lifestyle is a good balance to improve metabolic health, experts agree. (iStock)
Cole said he supports wider access to peptides, but emphasized the importance of transparency, product purity and clear labeling so healthcare professionals and consumers can make informed decisions.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Despite those concerns, Cole said he believes GLP-1s also hold significant therapeutic promise, citing their potential to reduce inflammation, help manage autoimmune conditions and improve gut health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"But again, what's the lowest dose that yields a beneficial result paired with lifestyle? I think that's where peptides can really shine," he said.
"And I am actually more excited about some of these other [peptides], like the inflammation ones or the longevity peptides."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Pope Leo visits site of miracle cures, meets people whose unexplained healings stunned doctors
summary: Pope Leo XIV prayed at the Massabielle Grotto and planned to meet with miracle cure recipients, sexual abuse victims and the sick during his Lourdes visit.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the miracles of Lourdes, Pope Leo XIV's expected visit there, and kratom as authorities await the toxicology reports in the deaths of two Ole Miss students on 'America Reports.'
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes from Paris on Saturday evening for his first-ever visit to the renowned place of miracle cures.
Back in 1858, a 14-year-old peasant girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported having 18 visions of the Virgin Mary at the Lourdes Massabielle Grotto. This ultimately led to her being named a saint.
The pope prayed at the Grotto Saturday night before leading an open-air Mass on the Prairie on Sunday, with hundreds of thousands expected to be in attendance.
POPE LEO DRAWS STAGGERING 800,000 FAITHFUL TO HEART OF PARIS FOR MASSIVE OUTDOOR MASS
He also planned to meet with bishops, the sick and the support staff.
I spoke with Dr. Alessandro de Franciscis, who recently retired as president of the Lourdes Office of Medical Observation after 17 years of reviewing treatments and possible miracle cures.
Pope Leo XIV presides over Mass at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in Lourdes, France.  (AP Images)
He discussed his upcoming meeting with the pope, who he said was visiting Lourdes in the name of purification and healing, including healing from the Church's recent sexual abuse scandals.
JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

"I think I love him," he told me. "I think he's doing very well (as pope). He's talking of the challenges that we have. You must have heard about his first encyclical letter on artificial intelligence ... all the good that this technology can bring to today's world. He's a guy from Chicago. I love him. We all love him!"
Priests sit before a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, France, on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (AP Images)
Dr. de Franciscis said the pope would meet with people whose miracle healings were investigated and later recognized by the Church.

Those include Sister Bernadette Moriau, who was cured of a spinal condition and was able to walk again, and Antonietta Raco, who in 2009 was cured of the severe neurodegenerative disease primary lateral sclerosis.

"He's also going to meet with a young woman (Delizia Cirolli) who was cured when she was only 7 years old of a Ewing's Sarcoma, a right knee cancer, back in the late '70s."
But for Lourdes, as well as for the pope, spiritual and physical healing lead to both minor and major miracles, according to de Franciscis.

He also spoke with me for my new book, "The Angels Among Us," about the hospitaliers, the aptly named "angels of Lourdes," who care for the sick there.
Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, France, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026.  (AP Images)

In the book, de Franciscis emphasizes the vital role of the hospitaliers, as well as the fact that much of the healing associated with visits to Lourdes and the Grotto is spiritual and often goes unrecognized — remaining below the radar.
"These so-called spiritual cures are so, so much more numerous than the physical ones that we know."

"I think that statistically, these so-called spiritual cures are so, so much more numerous than the physical ones that we know," he said to me from Lourdes, as he eagerly anticipated the pope’s visit.

"People come here to serve, they think they come here to help others — and instead they come out of this experience being so much better," de Franciscis went on.

"And they go back to their work and their lives and their families, and they're so relieved, I would say, they've really changed. So I think this aspect is very, very interesting."
In Lourdes this weekend, in the name of repentance and accountability, the pope also planned to sit down with seven victims of sexual assault committed by clergy of the Church.

title: Forgetting names and losing keys may signal something other than dementia
summary: Dr. Tommy Wood breaks down memory's three neurological stages and why noticing your own forgetfulness is actually a good sign, not an Alzheimer's flag.
story: Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said minor forgetfulness is often caused by fatigue or stress rather than the beginnings of a neurodegenerative disease.

Everyday memory lapses, like misplaced keys or forgotten names, are often overinterpreted as early signs of dementia, but neuroscience experts say actual early cognitive changes may be reversible if addressed promptly.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said minor forgetfulness is often caused by fatigue or stress rather than the beginnings of a neurodegenerative disease.

"For most people, it's just because you're stressed or you're tired and weren't paying attention," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong New York, the city's largest annual fitness and wellness festival.
DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS
"If you want to remember something ... you need to actually be focused, be paying attention. You need to tell your brain it's important to remember it."
Understanding memory loss
Wood said memory formation works in three stages: encoding (forming a memory), consolidation (storing it) and retrieval (accessing it).
Cognitive changes during aging are not inevitable, and taking proactive lifestyle steps early can help maintain or even restore brain function. (iStock)
When someone is stressed or sleep-deprived, the issue is typically retrieval, he said — the memory exists in the brain, but the individual struggles to access it in the moment.
In contrast, people experiencing a neurodegenerative disease often fail to encode the memory in the first place.
‘MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON’ HERO SULLY SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER’S WARNING SIGNS HE MISSED YEARS AGO
"They don't even remember or notice that there's something going on," Wood said. "If you're noticing something's not quite right, that's usually a good sign."
Preventable risk factors and reversibility

Dementia is clinically defined as the loss of cognitive function that's severe enough to impair an individual's ability to manage daily life independently. Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia account for 70% to 90% of cases, with many individuals showing signs of both.
Research indicates that at least 50% of dementia cases can be prevented by modifying lifestyle and health risk factors.
True memory problems stem from a failure to encode new memories in the brain, whereas stress-related forgetfulness is merely an issue with retrieving existing memories. (iStock)
Key preventable risk factors include heart and metabolic health problems, as well as hearing and vision loss.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Wood emphasized that addressing physical health issues — such as obtaining hearing aids or undergoing cataract surgery — directly lessens cognitive decline risk.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you expect decline, you won't do the things that will prevent decline from happening," Wood told Fox News Digital. "Believing that it's possible means you'll actually engage in these processes, and then through that, you can prevent a lot of this decline."
Minor memory lapses, like forgetting keys or names, are usually caused by stress or fatigue rather than early dementia, the expert said. (iStock)

Wood's focus on reversible causes of cognitive symptoms aligns with guidance from Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic, which note that several treatable medical conditions can mimic early dementia symptoms or contribute to subjective cognitive decline.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Common reversible causes include the following.

Vitamin deficiencies: Low levels of vitamin B12 or B1, which are essential for nerve and brain functionEndocrine disruption: Thyroid problems, particularly hypothyroidism, which slows brain metabolismMedication side effects: Interactions from sedative drugs, anticholinergics or polypharmacy in older adultsMental health conditions: Depression and severe anxiety, which can cause "pseudodementia," a state of cognitive slowing and memory lapse that resolves with mental health treatmentMetabolic and kidney issues: Chronic kidney or liver failure, as well as electrolyte imbalances, which alter levels of brain chemicals
Vitamin deficiencies: Low levels of vitamin B12 or B1, which are essential for nerve and brain function
Endocrine disruption: Thyroid problems, particularly hypothyroidism, which slows brain metabolism
Medication side effects: Interactions from sedative drugs, anticholinergics or polypharmacy in older adults
Mental health conditions: Depression and severe anxiety, which can cause "pseudodementia," a state of cognitive slowing and memory lapse that resolves with mental health treatment
Metabolic and kidney issues: Chronic kidney or liver failure, as well as electrolyte imbalances, which alter levels of brain chemicals
Managing physical health issues — such as controlling high blood pressure, treating vision or hearing loss and staying physically active — directly reduces cognitive decline risks. (iStock)
Cleveland Clinic highlights that early clinical intervention is critical when individuals notice changes in "brain fog" or executive function.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"How your brain functions on a day-to-day basis is kind of the output of everything your brain is dealing with," said Wood. "But if you start to notice something, there's still time to make some changes if you need to."
