title: Trump Pentagon launches competition for America's next great military base
summary: The winning state for the base site will be selected through a merit-based competition based on land, housing, schools, community support and regulatory cooperation.
story: Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon plans to select a state to host the first new U.S. military base built in 40 years.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday announced plans to build a modern, self-sustaining military fortress, saying the site will be selected through a merit-based competition among governors pitching their states as potential locations.
The megaproject, dubbed the "Next Great American Base," was unveiled during an address at Marine Corps Base Quantico as part of Hegseth’s six strategies to modernize the military.
The initiative rejects what Hegseth described as the legacy approach to spend heavily on advanced weapons systems while service members live on aging bases with outdated barracks.

"For too long, our military has been bogged down by the same old tired Washington playbook: spending trillions on exquisite weapons systems, while our troops live in aging bases, outdated barracks, and with inadequate infrastructure. That era is over," Hegseth said.
EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP
FILE — Hegseth said the project will replace aging military infrastructure with a modern base built from the ground up for troops and their families. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
"To back up our warfighters, when we bring the troops home, we won’t just reshuffle troops onto legacy posts. We are going to build them beautiful new bases from the ground up," he added.
The ambitious undertaking will feature a brand-new military installation spanning hundreds of thousands of acres and housing up to 25,000 service members.
"We are talking hundreds of thousands of acres with organic power generation, modern air defenses, and cutting edge technology — a fortress," he said.

The installation is expected to provide first-class living conditions, high-end training grounds and essential services such as health care and child care, while operating entirely off the commercial grid with independent power sources.

Hegseth added that the base will support President Donald Trump’s executive order on "Beautiful Civic Architecture," which calls for federal public buildings and military installations to be designed in timeless and classical styles.
"We owe our warriors nothing less than the gold standard," Hegseth said.
SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES MERIT-BASED MILITARY PROMOTIONS, TARGETS BIDEN-ERA DEI POLICIES
FILE — U.S. soldiers take part in a military ceremony. The proposed base, dubbed the "Next Great American Base," would house up to 25,000 service members.

To determine the site location, the Department of War said it is launching a transparent, merit-based competition in which state governors can pitch their proposals directly to top military leadership at the Pentagon.

The winning state will be chosen based on its ability to remove regulatory hurdles and bureaucracy to speed up construction, while offering the best package of land, community support, top-tier housing, schools and other services.

"The state that cuts the most red tape and offers the best package of land and support will win the historic honor of hosting the most lethal, modern, and beautiful military installation on the planet," a press release stated.
Pitch deliberations will be recorded and made public to eliminate "political favoritism," according to the Pentagon.

"No backroom Washington deals. No political favoritism – just a straight-up, merit-based contest to see which state will partner with us to build the most modern, beautiful, and lethal military installation on the planet," Hegseth said.

FILE - President Donald Trump sits next to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. The War Department says the winning state must cut red tape while offering a strong package of land, housing, schools and community support. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The project is the fourth announcement among six major strategic initiatives unveiled by the secretary.

According to the Department of War, the other initiatives focus on restoring male physical standards and combat roles, improving the comprehensive review of military standards, overhauling complaint processes, reforming senior leadership and focusing on core training and maintenance.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Unearthed clip exposes the Talarico comment that triggered backlash from parents
summary: James Talarico, the Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate, dismissed parents' concerns about pornography in schools as a "conspiracy theory" at a 2022 hearing.
story: James Talarico, speaking at a committee hearing on public education in 2022, waves off concerns about critical race theory, pornography in school materials. (Credit: Texas House of Representatives)

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once dismissed public outcry about explicit material in Texas public schools as a kind of "conspiracy theory" at a July 2022 hearing on education.

"We’re going to spend hours hearing bills that are just kind of conspiracy theory-driven and kind of kooky stuff. And we’re going to hear some of that today, I think, in the public testimony — not the invited testimony, but the public testimony," Talarico said then as a member of the Texas House of Representatives.

The resurfaced moment adds to the pile of past statements dealing with gender, immigration and law enforcement, complicating the political calculus for Talarico as he aims to convince voters in Texas that, even as a Democrat, he could represent a Republican-leaning constituency in the Lone Star State.
TED CRUZ, CONSERVATIVES RESPOND AFTER TALARICO CRITICIZES BIBLE-RELATED EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS AS 'PROPAGANDA'
James Talarico, D-Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, speaks at a campaign event in Round Rock, Texas, March 3, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
At the time of the 2022 hearing, many parents were raising concerns about news that schools and libraries across the country were featuring explicit materials that bordered on pornography.

In particular, an Ashland, Ohio, board meeting made news after a group of angry parents highlighted graphic illustrations from books like "It’s Perfectly Normal," "Making a Baby," "Own Your Period" and "Puberty is Gross but Also Really Awesome," all titles featuring some level of sexual references.
Similar outcries emerged in Kentucky, Oregon and North Carolina.

In Texas, state Rep. Matt Krause, a Republican, sparked similar backlash when he circulated a list of roughly 800 titles he believed were inappropriate for students. He expressed his alarm in a letter to Texas school districts.

"I am writing to you as the Chairman of the Texas House Committee on General Investigation," Krause wrote. "The committee may initiate inquiries concerning any ‘matter the committee considers necessary for the information of the legislature or for the welfare and protection of state citizens.’

"Please identify any other books or content in your district, specifying the campus location and funds spent on acquisition that address or contain … sexually explicit images, graphic presentations of sexual behavior that is in violation of the law or contain material that might make students feel discomfort, guilt, anguish or any other form of psychological distress because of their race or sex or convey that a student, by virtue of their race or sex is inherently racist sexist or oppressive whether consciously or unconsciously."
CONTROVERSIAL TEACHER TRAINING TARGETS PARENTAL AUTHORITY AS OPPRESSION, EDUCATION EXPERT WARNS
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Cailloux Theater Aug. 31, 2026, in Kerrville, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
In January 2022, several counties began evaluating their own books, leading some, like Granbury Independent School District, to pull 130 titles from shelves.

By July, the issue had made its way before the Texas Legislature in the form of an "interim charge," made by Republican Texas House Speaker Dade Phelan. It was a kind of exhortation for lawmakers to examine the issue, charging them to "monitor and analyze the state policy on curriculum and instructional materials used in public schools."
As a part of the Committee on Public Education, Talarico received the charge but expressed reservations about its substance, making his "conspiracy theory" comment.
He went on to ask Texas Education Agency Commissioner Mike Morath about the issue.
"I want to ask you about curriculum in Texas, of course, critical race theory, pornography; these are the things we see bubbling up on social media that’s going to be discussed here," Talarico said.
"Are you aware of any curriculum in the state of Texas that, one, bullies students based on their race or, two, grooms students with pornography?"
Morath, after noting that Texas is a very big state and the issue is "very complex," gave his blunt assessment.
"The answer is yes," Morath said.

"We have complaints that would appear to substantiate periodic problems in those areas, arguably. I can’t tell you it’s widespread. We’ve reviewed, in some cases, materials that were made available to students that I think the common citizen would agree would be inappropriate."
CARVILLE ADVISES TALARICO 'TO DEAL WITH' PAST CULTURE WAR COMMENTS IF HE WANTS TO WIN TEXAS
Democratic Texas State Rep. James Talarico speaks during a campaign launch rally Sept. 9, 2025, in Round Rock, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Even after the testimony, Talarico challenged the idea that explicit materials in schools were widespread.
"I would characterize as a conspiracy theory that’s being raised is that these are systemic policy problems in the state of Texas," Talarico said.
Following Talarico’s remarks, parents spoke out against his characterization.

"I actually drove in last night, so I’ve been here a very long time. And hopefully my comments and testimony today aren’t gonna be as ‘kooky’ as Representative Talarico had stated it was gonna be," one parent quipped.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Talarico’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: GOP challenger tears into Dem's 'moderate' image: 'Votes with the squad 90% of the time'
summary: Scott Singer, GOP candidate in FL-25, denounces Democrat incumbent Rep. Jared Moskowitz's voting record, alliance with "the squad," and calls into question his support for Israel.
story: The former Boca Raton mayor points to strong economic results, shifting demographics, and Moskowitz’s voting record as key levers for flipping the 25th District.

Republican congressional candidate Scott Singer is making the case that party, not just policy, will be decisive in his closely watched South Florida showdown with Democrat Rep. Jared Moskowitz, arguing that the incumbent’s moderate, pro-Israel image is at odds with his voting record and the direction of the Democrat Party.

Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton, told Fox News Digital that he believes his record of cutting taxes and reducing crime at the local level, combined with unwavering support for Israel, gives voters a clear contrast in Florida’s newly redrawn 25th Congressional District.

"Well, it is a tough cycle, but people understand the real Jared Moskowitz, one who votes with the squad 90% of the time, voted to put [Rep.] Ilhan Omar [D-Minn.] on the Foreign Affairs Committee, has passed no bills in Congress, but traded $4.5 million worth of stocks since he's been there. This district, after redistricting, is now a Republican plus five district," Singer told Fox News Digital.
GOP'S SINGER 'VERY PREPARED' TO OUST DEM MOSKOWITZ IN TOSS-UP FLORIDA RACE THAT COULD DETERMINE HOUSE MAJORITY
Former Boca Raton GOP Mayor Scott Singer, left, is challenging Democrat incumbent U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz for Florida's 25th Congressional District. (Getty Images)

"It takes in all of Boca Raton, where I was mayor for eight years, cut taxes, red tape, and crime, and goes down to Miami Beach, where I was born, and Fort Lauderdale, where I was raised," he continued. "Moskowitz doesn't live in the district, he's not from the district.

"But beyond that, the Republican plus five, a trend in Jewish voters, of which we have 25% … in our district, moving more conservatively, and people who are opposed to socialism and communism, which he will not denounce, understand that this is a critical race for House leadership, and they want someone like me, a local leader with a record of results."
Singer's business-friendly fiscal conservatism is the cornerstone of his campaign, and provides the policy framework for his priorities on Capitol Hill.

"Well, it gives me the record of results one would need. As mayor of Boca Raton, not only did we have the lowest property tax rate of any full-service city in Florida, I cut the tax rate seven times. I cut red tape, 21 streamlining initiatives," he said. "I cut crime by more than 25% from what were 40-year lows. Those are a record of results that people can relate to, because we improved the quality of life, improved the job base, lowered taxes, and made our streets safer."
UNEARTHED AUDIT EXPOSES VULNERABLE DEM'S HANDLING OF COVID RELIEF FUNDS: 'GROSS OVERSIGHT'
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., speaks during a news conference in Washington, D.C. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Congressional Integrity Project, File)

Singer continued: "That's what we want right now in America. We want secure borders, not like the porous borders that Jared Moskowitz supported under [former] President [Joe] Biden that have increased crime and ravaged communities. They want tax relief, not the tax hike that he voted for. $4 trillion, including taxes on Social Security, tipped workers, small businesses and families that are hurting. Now he's trying to come around with a modest talk of the gas tax reduction.
"He had the chance to vote on taxes and repeatedly has voted for higher taxes. People want a leader with a record of results. That's what I bring."
While Moskowitz has carefully cultivated a moderate image during his tenure in Congress, Singer disputes that characterization.

"No, he's not. He's been voting in lockstep. He's already said he'll vote for whoever the Democratic leadership is. And you can see that we'll have committee chairs like [Rep.] Rashida Tlaib [D-Mich.] and AOC [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.], if heaven forbid, the Democrats win Congress," Singer said. "He already voted for Ilhan Omar on Foreign Affairs, despite his talking about her statements being bad, he voted to keep her in charge of foreign affairs in our country."
FLORIDA GOP NOMINEE BLASTS 20-YEAR DEM INCUMBENT AS A ‘SOCIALIST’ RUBBER-STAMP WITH ‘PRECIOUS LITTLE TO SHOW’
Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., speaks on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo, File)

Added Singer: "He's voted for tax hikes again … He says he's strong on Israel, but he voted against US-Israeli cooperation, when other Democrats were willing to cross the aisle. And then just a few weeks ago, he would not denounce socialism, even though other Democrats would. He's trying to have it out both ways, but his record is really Democratic, really liberal, 90% with the squad."
Both Moskowitz and Singer both position themselves as strong supporters of Israel, but Singer argues that membership in today's Democrat Party makes effective advocacy for Israel difficult.

"I'm a stronger supporter for Israel. I would never have put Ilhan Omar on the Foreign Affairs Committee. I would not have, like he did, voted against U.S.-Israel cooperation in the NDAA [National Defense Authorization Act]," Singer said. "I would have not voted to undercut President [Donald] Trump's efforts and our military's efforts with the War Powers Act vote months ago when the U.S. and Israel were fighting against a common enemy.

"He's done all of those things because Democratic leadership requires him. And he admitted three weeks ago to Jewish Insider that he's being ostracized in his own party. He doesn't have any more chits to give in. He has to go with the way the majority is going, and that expanded squad is going to tamp out any voice he has.
People leave after casting their vote during early voting in Miami Beach, Fla. (David Santiago/Miami Herald via AP)

"In my party, support for Israel is a feature, not a bug, and I don't have to moderate my views or vote in accordance with the majority…I can be a strong supporter for Israel without reservation. Jared's admitted he can't be and won't be."
Finally, while Singer said he is a strong supporter of the Trump administration's military engagement in Iran, he would like to see an end to the conflict soon.

"I think we need to have a resolution of this. I think we need to emerge victoriously. We have to remember that nuclear Iran is an existential threat," he said. "We have seen how dastardly, vicious, murderous this regime has been over 47 years. Their foreign policy is death to America. They've killed Americans, they'll kill more.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And even since this conflict started, they've started attacking other nations who weren't combatants trying to widen the conflict. They support terror across the world. It's hurt America, it's hurt Americans, it's hurt our allies like Israel, and it's hurting the free world. We need to stop this.
"And I am optimistic we'll see a resolution soon. And that's a small price to pay. Even if we have some hiccups there, it's a smaller price to pay to ensure Iran does not have a nuclear weapon."
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: 'Drug-dealing' network shielded by blue states targeted in SCOTUS challenge
summary: Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill filed two lawsuits targeting blue-state shield laws and the online abortion pill pipeline.
story: Louisiana, Alabama and Arkansas are challenging shield laws they say block investigations into abortion-pill providers accused of sending medication across state lines.

Louisiana Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill is escalating her fight against abortion pills entering states that ban abortions through two lawsuits — one targeting the providers accused of distributing the drugs and another challenging the blue-state laws shielding them from prosecution.

Murrill, along with Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin, sued New York, California and Massachusetts at the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging their shield laws block cooperation with investigations into abortion-pill providers. The attorneys general also filed a separate lawsuit in Louisiana against more than 30 people and organizations accused of advertising, prescribing, dispensing or shipping abortion pills into their states.
"This is drug dealing and it's illegal," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And we're going to continue to do everything that we can to enforce the laws in our states."

The two lawsuits, filed Wednesday, are the latest move in a widening state-by-state fight over abortion. That conflict has grown since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which struck down Roe v. Wade and gave elected officials the power to set abortion policy in their states.
HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS
A container holding boxes of Mifepristone, the first medication in a medical abortion, at Alamo Women's Clinic in Carbondale, Ill., April 20, 2023. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
Murrill said the Supreme Court case targets the blue states' legal protections that have thwarted Louisiana's previous efforts to prosecute out-of-state doctors.

"These shield laws are very comprehensive," Murrill said, arguing that California and New York prohibit officials from assisting other states seeking to enforce judgments stemming from abortion-related conduct.

Louisiana has already indicted New York physician Margaret Carpenter and California physician Remy Coeytaux over allegations that they prescribed abortion drugs that were sent into Louisiana. New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom have refused to extradite the doctors.

The Supreme Court complaint cited Louisiana's unsuccessful effort to extradite Carpenter, saying Hochul declared there was "no way in hell" she would comply with Louisiana's request. The filing said New York later strengthened its shield law, including by allowing prescribers of abortion drugs to keep their names off prescription labels.
In response to the lawsuit, Hochul said she will continue fighting to ensure New York remains a "safe haven for reproductive rights."

"No one should have to fear being punished for seeking or providing reproductive care," Hochul said in a statement. "As anti-abortion extremists in other states try to reach across our borders and threaten patients and providers, New York will stand up for them. Our shield laws are there to protect that freedom."
Newsom similarly rejected Louisiana's request to extradite Coeytaux in January, saying California would not help other states punish doctors for providing abortion access that is legal in California.
CALIFORNIA ABORTION PILL SUPPLIERS PLOT WORKAROUNDS AHEAD OF SUPREME COURT MIFEPRISTONE DECISION
When Murrill vowed to sue, Newsom responded on X telling her to "Go f--- yourself. California will never help you criminalize healthcare."

"I think that if I sent guns into their states illegally, they would certainly try to come after me," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "I said specifically at the time that we would be coming for them and we are."
"We are going to take down those laws using every tool that we have at our disposal," she continued.
The second lawsuit directly targets what Murrill calls the "pill pipeline."

The 100-page complaint alleges providers used online questionnaires to obtain information from customers before abortion drugs were mailed into states where their distribution is prohibited. The states allege some organizations openly acknowledged that their conduct violated those states' laws while relying on shield laws to protect themselves from legal consequences.
Murrill said investigators have conducted controlled purchases and received pills packaged in small bags, sometimes in quantities she said exceeded what would ordinarily be prescribed.
"We've seen it for ourselves," Murrill said. "There's no supervision, there's no healthcare, there's no communication whatsoever. It's all done online."

Murrill argued that the system can allow people other than pregnant women to obtain the drugs, pointing to cases Louisiana authorities said involved women being pressured or deceived into taking abortion medication.
PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND

"We have a situation in one town in Louisiana that we've documented and investigated where a father did not want his teenage daughter to keep a pregnancy," Murrill told Fox News Digital. "And so he basically put the medication in a smoothie, forced her to drink it. She did ultimately give birth to that baby at 23 weeks and is still in a NICU fighting for its life."
The attorney general also said Louisiana wants more help from the Trump administration.
"Obviously we think the FDA could be doing more and we've asked them to do that," Murrill said.
Louisiana has separately challenged federal rules that eliminated an in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone.

Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser backed the litigation, accusing blue states of using their laws "to obstruct justice" and urging the Justice Department to settle Louisiana's separate FDA litigation.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Democrats’ pro-abortion extremism has brought this country to a crisis point. Abortion activists flagrantly sell dangerous drugs across state lines and women and children pay the price, with more and more survivors of ‘death in a pill’ bravely coming forward," Dannenfelser said in a statement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to New York, California and Massachusetts' governors' offices for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Blanche announces charges against 10 permanent residents accused of Minnesota voter fraud
summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced indictments of 10 lawful permanent residents accused of noncitizen voting in Minnesota elections since 2022.
story: Attorney General Todd Blanche said nine lawful permanent residents illegally voted in Minnesota federal elections, with most of them falsely claiming to be U.S. citizens.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that a federal grand jury had indicted ten lawful permanent residents accused of voting illegally or attempting to do so in multiple Minnesota elections, including the state’s August 2026 primary.

The ten defendants, originally from Liberia, Canada, South Africa, Brazil, Bosnia, Germany, Ghana and Lithuania, allegedly lied to election officials and told them they were U.S. citizens so they could register to vote.
They were accused of voting in the 2022 and 2024 general elections, according to court records.

"Voter fraud erodes the public's trust in our electoral system, and it's vital to our democratic process that we do everything that we can to restore that trust," Blanche said at a news conference announcing the charges.
FEDERAL INDICTMENT HANDED DOWN IN MINNESOTA RELATED TO ISSUE SOME DEMS CLAIM NEVER HAPPENS: 'HOTBED FOR FRAUD'

"The most basic way the Department of Justice can accomplish this restoration of trust is by working to make sure the only people voting in an election in the United States are American citizens who are eligible to vote."

Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks alongside U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen during a news conference Sept. 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C., announcing the arrest of 10 people for allegedly voting illegally in elections in Minnesota. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The 10 defendants were charged separately. They are Bhator Konah Bryant, 61, of Liberia; Edvile Vaidoto Edmunds, 59, of Lithuania; Joshua Frederick Kofi Edzie, 63, of Ghana; Alan Barbu Kargbo, 48, of Liberia; Paul Kras, 78, of Germany; Fadil Rasim Ozegovic, 58, of Bosnia; Aparecido Donizetti Padovan, 62, of Brazil; Chris Adam Pettiquoi, 43, of Liberia; Christian Liam Schenk, 47, of Canada; and Hester Sophia Weihmann, 69, of South Africa.
Bryant appears to be the only defendant who wasn't charged with voting illegally, only falsely claiming citizenship in 2024 to register.

Making a false citizenship claim to vote is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, while voting by a noncitizen is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in prison and a $100,000 fine.
Blanche also expressed frustration that the media has, in his view, not taken the Justice Department's work prosecuting election fraud cases seriously to this point.
Officers with Homeland Security Investigations stand on either side of Alan Barbu Kargbo, a 48-year-old Liberian national who allegedly voted illegally in the 2024 election. (Department of Justice)
BIDEN ADMINISTRATION GRANTED WOMAN GREEN CARD MONTHS BEFORE SHE ILLEGALLY VOTED IN 2024 ELECTION: DHS

"I don't know what the number is that will work for you guys. Whether it's 106, maybe it's 120," he said, referring to a hypothetical number of investigations. "At some point, it has to become meaningful to to the media."

Blanche said since President Donald Trump has returned to office, the Justice Department has charged more than 90 people with voter fraud offenses, including 50 illegal immigrants in the past five weeks.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there have been 10 voter fraud-related convictions and that there are more than 1,600 active investigations into similar conduct across the country.

Mullin did not answer a reporter’s question about how the department plans to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database, known as SAVE, to identify voters who may be ineligible ahead of the midterms.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on Sept. 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS

The Supreme Court ruled Friday that the administration may use the database for voter-eligibility checks while litigation continues. SAVE has historically been used to help government agencies verify whether noncitizens applying for public benefits are eligible to receive them.

States’ use of the SAVE database is voluntary, but federal law generally bars states from conducting systematic voter-roll purges within 90 days of a federal election. With the midterms less than a month away, the Supreme Court’s ruling is expected to have limited immediate impact.

During the same news conference Wednesday, Blanche also announced that the Justice Department had filed a judicial misconduct complaint with the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals against several Minnesota federal judges who spoke with The New York Times about cases the department said were still pending.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents conduct immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis Jan. 28, 2026. (Madison Thorn/Anadolu via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The article, published Sept. 17, centered on an interview with Judge Patrick J. Schiltz, who said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violated nearly 100 orders from the federal district court in Minnesota during the height of Operation Metro Surge, which saw hundreds of federal agents in the streets of Minneapolis throughout January of this year.
Schiltz, a George W. Bush appointee, told the Times that the alleged violation of these orders likely came down to incompetence and staffing shortages at the Justice Department.
Blanche said Schiltz airing various complaints about the Trump administration to the Times was a violation of judicial canons and his ethical duties.

"We have asked the 8th Circuit to conduct an investigation, and in the meantime, we ask that these judges recuse themselves from every case involving DHS, either criminal or civil in nature, because of the obvious bias they have shown in this article," Blanche said.

Shiltz issued this response to Fox News, "As legal ethics experts have confirmed, I was acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times.  Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may ‘speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ That is exactly what I did."
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Republican glee erupts as White House boasts sharp decline in immigration from Muslim-majority nations
summary: A White House graph shows a 96% drop in legal immigration from Muslim-majority nations since 2024, but the Cato researcher behind it pushed back.
story: Former President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, D.C., criticizes current border policies. He highlights the claim of "zero illegal aliens" admitted in the last 13 months versus "25 million people" previously. Trump argues "Sleepy Joe Biden's ideology" is responsible for dangerous individuals, including murderers and drug dealers, entering the country, emphasizing the human cost of these "journeys through hell."
The political right celebrated after a White House X account posted a graph showing that legal immigration to the U.S. from nations with Muslim majority populations has all but halted.
The account highlighted a 96 percent cut in legal immigration from majority-Muslim countries since 2024 and attached a graph from the Cato Institute, a notoriously pro-immigration think tank.

The graph showed a drastic decline in quarterly admissions of immigrants from those countries beginning in January 2025, when President Donald Trump officially took office. It also declined in late 2024, the last year of former President Joe Biden's tenure in office.
AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

President Donald Trump pumps his fist as he steps off Air Force One upon arrival at Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Feb. 14, 2025, en route to his Mar-a-Lago resort. (Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images)

At its peak, immigration from Muslim-majority nations was over 22,000 people per month between July and October of 2024, according to the graph. But by the beginning of January of this year, that number had dropped to almost zero.
Online, the political right cheered the drastic shift.
"Absolutely incredible victory for the American people, thanks to POTUS," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, said.
"These are the wins we need to continue to deliver on," said Brandon Herrera, the GOP nominee for Congress in Texas' 23rd District.
"4 percent to go! Thank you, President Trump," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla.
"Let’s pump up those rookie numbers for every category of immigrant," columnist Kurt Schlichter said.

Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, arrives for the House Oversight and Government Reform Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past" in the Rayburn House Office Building on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY

Some turned the graph into a referendum on the results of Republican leadership, and urged conservatives to vote during the 2026 midterm elections despite concerns about cost-of-living, the Iran war, and other issues for which Trump has been knocked by members of his own party.
"I voted for this—and will again," said user David Harrison.
"The next time you get the urge to 'punish the GOP.' Remember that Democrats will reverse this overnight," said Turning Point Action's Ben Larrabee.
"People screaming that Trump and the GOP aren't doing anything about this problem [are] hardest hit, like squarely between the eyes," online personality James Lindsay said of the graph.
JONATHAN TURLEY: SUPREME COURT HANDS TRUMP A BORDER VICTORY LIBERALS CAN'T SPIN
"Vote like Western Civilization depends on it, because it does," said Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet.

Not everyone was thrilled with the decline in legal immigration from this demographic, though, including David J. Bier, who is the director of immigration studies at Cato and who took credit for the research behind the graph.

WASHINGTON, DC - JUNE 26: Activists protest on the anniversary of the Supreme Court's ruling upholding the Trump administration's restriction of travel to the U.S. from predominantly Muslin countries, on Capitol Hill June 26, 2019 in Washington, DC. The Court in a 5-4 ruling upheld a third version of the ban, which has also been applied to countries not predominantly Muslim. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images) (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)
"Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free, and less prosperous," he said in reply.
Despite Bier's claim, no court has decided that Trump's move to reduce immigration from Muslim-majority countries is "illegal," though there have been challenges in district courts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

During his first term in office, Trump faced a challenge to his proposed travel restrictions from Muslim-majority countries. The policy was enjoined by the federal district court for the District of Hawaii, and upheld by two federal appellate courts. However, the Supreme Court ultimately decided in Hawaii vs. Trump that Trump's policy was legal.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Dems kill Republican's chances of lowering Americans' electricity bills in key election flashpoint
summary: Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at making AI data centers bear rising electricity costs that Jon Husted championed.
story: Ohio Senate race candidates clash over local energy costs and AI data centers as the 'Fox News Sunday' panel analyzes the upcoming midterm elections. The panel debates the political stakes of high utility bills and Chinese bot farm manipulation on social media. New polling shows a tight Senate race in Maine.
Democrats blocked a push to tackle one of the key issues driving this midterm election cycle, and may have given a vulnerable Republican a political lifeline in the process.

Republicans’ effort to crack down on rising electricity costs caused by the boom in data centers across the country was stifled on Wednesday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats, despite cruising through the House in a massive bipartisan vote.

Schumer’s blockade, however, wasn't unanimous among Democrats, with four — Sens. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Maggie Hassan, D-N.H. — breaking ranks to support the bill.

The Ratepayer Protection Act, would have created a standard for AI companies and the data centers they run to bear the brunt of electricity costs — an issue that has become a predominant concern for voters this midterm cycle.
FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, speaks during a news conference following Senate Democratic policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 23, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
But Democrats argued it was a toothless effort that lacked any real enforcement mechanism, and merely a political ploy to give vulnerable Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, a boost.

"The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill."
"We need real action on data centers. And what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push force forward a bill that is totally optional?"

While the U.S. continues its arms race with China for AI dominance, voters want to see tech companies cool their jets and slow the rapid construction of data centers. A Fox News poll from July found that 70% of voters, both Republicans and Democrats, opposed the construction of new data centers.
SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS
Republicans, including Husted, hoped that voter concerns could persuade Democrats to break from Schumer and vote in favor of the bill heading into Wednesday’s test.
"We all know that people would like to see us do something to lower their prices," Husted said. We have the opportunity to do that."

Data centers have become a political cudgel against Husted in his race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has labeled him the "face of data centers" in a battle that could determine who wins the majority in November.

Husted argued that the bill passed the House with only three Democrats voting against it, and that this push didn’t need to be labeled a "partisan victory." Killing the bill, however, could give Husted a needed boost to campaign on, given that Democrats stopped one of the main issues voters have going into the election, particularly in Ohio.
"It's like, look, this can be an opportunity for the Democrats to join us and say, ‘yeah, we agree. We're gonna work with them to get something done,’ and I hope they will," Husted said.
ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, speaks to reporters following policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol Building on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Husted is pushing the Ratepayer Protection Act, which Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has called a fraud and a toothless messaging bill. (Getty Images)
But Democrats countered the legislation was just a stunt to give Husted political ammunition.
Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that voters could see through the politics being played with by the GOP, and that the bill is "good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them."

"Because it's not, it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said. "And so that's what we need. We need something that is actually gonna be substantial and meet the moment rather than things that are just designed to be able to help with political elections."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that it was a massive bipartisan effort in the House, and questioned "why you would say that" the effort was just a political front to give Husted an issue to campaign on.

"I just think, if you’re looking at issues that we want to get at the heart of what everybody seems to be saying, the Democrats and others are saying, are important, we're concerned about," Thune said. "And it's a chance to actually make the law, it’s not just making a point here."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Schumer tanks popular insider trading ban in Dem effort to derail Republican's agenda ahead of midterms
summary: Senate Democrats blocked a GOP bill combining a stock trading ban with voter ID requirements, with Chuck Schumer calling it "trickery" and "skullduggery."
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Senate Republicans initiating test votes to shield consumers from high utility rates tied to data centers and forcing Democrats on the record regarding the SAVE America Act voter identification requirements.
Senate Democrats shut down Republicans’ bid to deal with two key issues for voters heading into the midterms.

Republicans tried and failed to pass a bill that would marry differing policy issues: banning lawmakers from using their insider knowledge to trade stocks and implementing voter ID policy nationwide — the latter of which the GOP has so far failed to accomplish with their SAVE America Act.

The Stop Insider Trading Act cruised through the House earlier this month, where a majority of House Democrats voted against it. Though voters are highly supportive of both, Democrats in the House and Senate argued that the stock trade ban wasn’t strong enough, while the voter ID element was too aggressive.

But the efforts to shut down the votes appear to build on a growing trend ahead of the November midterms — Democrats don't want to hand Republicans two massive wins going into a must-win election for both parties.
SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the US Capitol in Washington, DC on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., argued that Republicans knew the bill would never pass, and that they "designed it that way."
"They don't want this bill to become law," Schumer insisted. "So they put a poison pill in that they knew would tank it."

"It's really trickery. Skullduggery," he added. "If Republican senators really cared about stopping stock trading by members, they wouldn't have loaded it up with a poison pill voter ID bill, which Senate Democrats have defeated already twice."
They are two issues, though worlds apart, that have routinely failed to launch in Congress.

Senate Democrats have blocked voter ID and the SAVE America Act — and its several iterations throughout the year — multiple times, while banning lawmakers from trading stocks has largely been stifled by intraparty quarrels on both sides of the aisle.
SCHUMER SAID ‘DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID’ — THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL
House Republicans are unhappy the legislation failed, too.

"No lawmaker should be able to profit off of insider information. I’ll continue my work to pass the Stop Insider Trading Act," House Administration Committee Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital. "I’m encouraged that 53 Senators voted to ban members of Congress from trading stocks this afternoon. Unfortunately, Senate Democrats filibustered this commonsense ethics reform."
Still, they are issues that Americans overwhelmingly support.

A poll from the University of Maryland published in 2023 found that 86% of Americans on both sides of the political spectrum supported banning lawmakers from trading stocks. And a 2025 poll from the Pew Research Center found that 83% of Americans favored "requiring all voters to show government-issued photo identification to vote."

It’s the first of two bills Republicans will try to pass on Wednesday to tackle voters’ concerns heading into the midterms, where President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and its effect on the economy, could make or break the GOP’s grip on power in both chambers.
DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., spoke with reporters as he headed to the Senate chamber at the U.S. Capitol on March 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
The stock trading bill was pushed by Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who is in a tightening bid for re-election.

The other bill will create standards for AI companies and data centers to bear the brunt of electricity costs, a key issue that has emerged in this midterm cycle that has candidates in battleground states scrambling to craft policy positions against the hulking, windowless structures.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

That bill is being pushed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is running in one of the most contested races this cycle. Democrats contend that the GOP's attempt to push through the data center bill is nothing more than a political lifeline for Husted's campaign.

"Both pieces of legislation strike at the very heart of issues that the American people care deeply about, passionately about," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "And we'll see if the Democrats are willing to take yes for an answer."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: GOP lawmaker’s fraud crusade takes dramatic turn as scandal engulfs his own career
summary: Utah State Rep. Trevor Lee, a Republican who championed anti-fraud bills and praised Nick Shirley, now faces mortgage fraud charges himself.
story: Vice President JD Vance announces a crackdown on alleged COVID-era relief fraud, including the suspension of more than 870,000 borrowers from loan programs. Vance also warns that individuals found to have defrauded taxpayers could face federal prosecution.
After spending years railing against fraud, Utah Republican state Rep. Trevor Lee has resigned after being charged with fraud himself.

The Utah Attorney General's Office filed criminal charges against Lee on Monday, accusing him of forging documents and engaging in fraud in order to obtain a home loan. Prior to the charges, Lee had pushed legislation aimed at combating unemployment fraud and publicly praised efforts to expose the sweeping fraud scandals that have rocked Minnesota in recent years.

In one video obtained by prosecutors, the CEO of a Utah water company "stated that Lee had requested cash advances totaling $93,000 to show increased income to assist in purchasing his home, and that Lee said he would make (the CEO) 'whole' by securing (his) company a government contract with Hill Air Force Base," according to the charging document.
SWING-STATE'S FRAUD RECKONING RAISES MINNESOTA-STYLE ALARM AS WILD SCHEMES EXPOSED
Flags fly at the Utah State Capitol in Salt Lake City on Jan. 18, 2026. (Sydney Schaefer/AP)
Another company claimed that Lee improperly used an offer letter from them to make it seem as if his income was higher than it was.

"Lee devised a scheme to obtain a $1 million home loan by false pretenses. To execute it, he communicated fraudulent documents to Kind Lending through the mortgage process — a forged Enevive employment contract, a loan application overstating his Enevive income, and a Blue Logic offer letter he knew misrepresented his employment," prosecutors wrote.
Former Utah state Rep. Trevor Lee in his official headshot.  (Utah House/UTleg.gov)

Investigators say Lee admitted during an interview that he personally forged the Enevive CEO’s signature on the employment contract to obtain the loan and knew the offer letter did not reflect income the company could actually pay him.
EXCLUSIVE: NICK SHIRLEY FIRES BACK AT MINNESOTA CRITICS: 'NUMBERS DON'T LIE, AND CONVICTIONS DON'T LIE'
Nick Shirley, YouTuber and independent journalist, testified before Congress Jan. 21 over Minnesota fraud scandal. (OutKick / Reuters)

Lee’s social media feed is full of positive references to Nick Shirley, a content creator who attracted national attention after releasing videos alleging fraud involving Somali-run childcare centers and other publicly funded programs in Minnesota.

"Nick is going to stop a Gavin Newsom presidency single handily (sic.)," Lee said in one post. In another post, Lee offered Shirley assistance after he was charged a fee for filming at the Utah state capital building.
"Keep up the good work Nick," Lee said in his most recent post directed at the YouTuber, dated July 11.
In addition to the praise of Shirley, Lee also introduced pieces of legislation designed to crack down on unemployment assistance fraud in 2023 and 2024.
BRAZEN SOCIAL MEDIA FRAUD SCHEMES WREAK HAVOC AS TRUMP OFFICIAL ISSUES STARK WARNING FOR 'FRAUDFLUENCERS'
Tourists visit the Utah State Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 11, 2025. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Lee resigned from the legislature shortly after the charges were filed.

"Due to personal circumstances that require my attention, I no longer feel I can give my constituents the time, attention and service they deserve," he said. "I will always be grateful for the people I have met, the relationships I have built and the opportunity I have had to serve the people of Utah."
Even if the fraud charges hadn’t come, Lee’s time in the legislature was approaching an end as he had lost his GOP primary election in June.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lee did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

title: Explosive sleeper issue could fuel midterm shakeups, top Republican predicts: ‘You’re gonna see surprises’
summary: Tom Emmer says fraud is the top issue driving Minnesota voters to the polls and predicts Republican "surprises" in several midterm elections.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to House Majority Whip Top Emmer about possible ‘surprises’ in November as fraud drives voters in both parties to the polls.

LEWISTON, MAINE - With just about a month left until the midterm elections, Rep. Tom Emmer (R-MN) told Fox News Digital that fraud is an issue motivating voters to the polls, and in Minnesota, his home state, he thinks the issue could yield some "surprises" at the ballot box.

"Fraud is a lot more important to the U.S. taxpayers than being a Republican or a Democrat," Emmer said. "People want good government. They want to know that they're paying for good government, that they are not having their hard-earned taxpayer dollars being siphoned off and stolen and sent out of the country. They're also asking, why hasn't anyone called this out and held these people accountable? And I think you're going to see that at the ballot box on November 3."

Emmer, the House Majority Whip, was in Maine with Republican House candidate Paul LePage, the first stop of his planned 56-district nationwide blitz across the United States, rallying voters for Republicans as the party tries to hold on their razor-thin majority in the House against daunting historical and political headwinds.

Emmer’s home state of Minnesota was the epicenter of fraud’s explosion into the national conversation late last year, prompting Gov. Tim Walz to abandon his re-election bid. Emmer expressed optimism that Republicans in Minnesota will resonate with voters on fraud in a state where a Republican hasn’t won a statewide election since 2006.
KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?'
Fox News Digital spoke to GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer about how the fraud issue will play with voters in November. (Fox News Digital/Paul Steinhauser)

"Fraud in Minnesota is the number one issue," Emmer said. "We've got a completely incompetent, I would argue corrupt in some instances, governor and an attorney general who took campaign funds from Somali fraudsters that he was actively trying to protect from getting caught in their fraud. This is a big deal for Minnesotans."

Emmer said voters are looking for an "honest system that actually works for the people" and not "the criminals" and the Republican candidates for Senate, governor, attorney general and auditor in Minnesota have all made fighting fraud a central issue of their campaigns.
NEW AUDIT IN WALZ'S BACKYARD EXPOSES MASSIVE FRAUD RISK TIED TO POST-GEORGE FLOYD ACTIVISM

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz testifies during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing at the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2026. The committee held the hearing to examine the alleged misuse of federal funds intended for Minnesota social services and Medicaid programs. (Getty Images)

"You easily could have Michelle Tafoya being the next U.S. Senator from the state of Minnesota, a Republican, you could have Lisa Demuth as the Republican governor and already, the attorney general candidate, Ron Schutz and the state auditor candidate Scott Jensen, the polling showing that they are leading," Emmer said. "So yes, Minnesota is going to be one of those places where you see surprises. I think you're gonna see surprises in Michigan as well and other places all across the country."

Emmer sat down for a roundtable discussion on fraud with LePage, Maine’s former governor running for Congress in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, where the Minnesota Republican railed against the lack of accountability for fraud in his home state.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., joins Maine GOP House candidate Paul LePage at a fraud roundtable in Lewiston, Maine, on Sept. 29, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

"They need to be held accountable and that's the one thing that's missing again in Minnesota. You've got all of these fraudsters being charged and convicted, not one public official has been charged at all, and that's got to change, and I hope it changes in Maine and other places, because it's high time that people be held accountable for ripping off the generous American people," Emmer told the panel.

The Trump administration has made combating fraud a central focus this year, creating a Justice Department Fraud Division and a White House task force led by Vice President JD Vance. The White House says the task force has uncovered roughly $245.7 billion in fraud since its creation, while also stopping an additional $62.9 billion annually and enforcing $59.1 billion through criminal charges, settlements and penalties.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Secret phone record seizure sparks personal lawsuit from GOP senator
summary: Marsha Blackburn's lawsuit targets Jack Smith personally, arguing the special counsel was never lawfully appointed and violated her constitutional rights.
story: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., discusses his heated clash with former special counsel Jack Smith during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on ‘America Reports.’

FIRST ON FOX: A top Republican senator whose phone toll records were secretly subpoenaed during Jack Smith's investigation of President Donald Trump sued the former special counsel in his personal capacity Wednesday, arguing he was never lawfully empowered to wield the authority behind the Arctic Frost investigation.

The lawsuit, Senator Marsha Blackburn v. John L. Smith, argues the prosecutor lacked lawful authority to serve as special counsel and violated the lawmaker's rights by obtaining the records. Blackburn is asking a federal court to declare Smith's appointment unconstitutional, order the records destroyed and award $1 in nominal damages.

The case therefore seeks to test not only Smith’s tactics, but the legitimacy of the authority he claims to have exercised as special counsel appointed by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland during the Biden administration.

"This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation’s justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people," Blackburn, R-Tenn., told Fox News Digital.
JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION

Jack Smith, former US special counsel, arrives for a closed-door deposition before the House Judiciary Committee in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Dec. 17, 2025. Smith was subpoenaed to testify about his sweeping investigations into President Donald Trump's actions, as part of an ongoing investigation the panel is conducting into the probes he led. Photographer: Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Through his Arctic Frost witch-hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the president of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation’s history," she said.

Blackburn’s suit argues that Smith lacked lawful authority to hold the office he purported to exercise, while separately seeking to impose personal liability on him for the way that purported authority was used against her.
JACK SMITH THRUST BACK INTO SPOTLIGHT AT BLANCHE HEARING OVER EXPOSED SENATORS’ MESSAGES

Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., speaks as U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi testifies before the Senate Judiciary Committee in the Hart Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on Oct. 7, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

The case opens a new legal front against Smith one day after his contentious Senate Judiciary Committee testimony, during which he acknowledged approving subpoenas for members of Congress despite understanding that nondisclosure orders prevented them from challenging the seizures under the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause.

Smith is a longtime prosecutor who most recently served as special counsel overseeing the Justice Department's investigations into President Donald Trump. Earlier in his career, he prosecuted cases before the International Criminal Court and led the DOJ's Public Integrity Section, which brought bribery charges against former Virginia Republican Gov. Robert F. McDonnell in a case where the Supreme Court later unanimously vacated the conviction.

Arctic Frost was the codename for the FBI investigation into Trump's handling of classified documents and alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election before the probe was handed over to Smith by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland.

Blackburn and her data were swept up in the probe after Smith's team subpoenaed toll records from her and several other Republicans—a move that sparked outrage at Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing over whether obtaining the records without notification violated the Constitution.

In May 2023, Smith’s office issued a grand-jury subpoena seeking Verizon toll records, while a separate nondisclosure order barred the company from notifying affected customers—including Blackburn—that its information had been turned over.

While the records did not reveal the contents of conversations, they showed whom Blackburn communicated with, when and for how long, according to the complaint. The lawsuit alleges that Smith’s office obtained a court-approved nondisclosure order without informing the judge that the subpoena sought records belonging to a sitting U.S. senator.
JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS
Former Special Counsel John L. "Jack" Smith, left; Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tennessee, right. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images; Brian Stukes/Getty Images)

More broadly, Smith’s team issued 197 subpoenas to 34 individuals and 163 businesses seeking information involving at least 430 Republican individuals and entities, according to Senate Judiciary Committee records.

Tuesday’s hearing also began with a scathing rebuke from Chairman Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, who accused Smith’s prosecutors of sweeping up communications between journalists at Fox News and other media organizations and sources connected to the first Trump administration.

For his part, Smith repeatedly hit back at allegations of corrupt or partisan prosecution, saying at one point his "investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation."
Blackburn's suit is being brought by the nonpartisan New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA) on her behalf, and the Tennessee senator thanked the group for its partnership.
JACK SMITH'S SENATE PHONE RECORDS PROBE TURNS TO VERIZON'S HANDLING OF SUBPOENAS

Blackburn’s attorneys argue that Smith exercised special counsel powers without lawful constitutional or statutory authorization. Separately, the complaint names Smith in his personal capacity and seeks to hold him liable for alleged violations of Blackburn’s constitutional and civil rights arising from the subpoena and nondisclosure order.

"Jack Smith was illegally named Special Counsel in November of 2022, with Attorney General Merrick Garland handing a private citizen the sweeping powers of a special counsel," NCLA said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.
"Then-President Biden did not nominate Smith, nor did the Senate confirm Smith as either Special Counsel or in any other position. And no statute authorized his appointment."

"NCLA’s complaint asks the court to declare Smith’s appointment unlawful under the Constitution’s Appointments Clause and to hold Smith accountable, in his personal capacity, for his gross abuses of power."
VETERAN DEM BREAKS PARTY LINE AS JACK SMITH SPYING SCANDAL GRIPS CAPITOL HILL

The suit alleges the subpoena violated Blackburn’s constitutional and civil rights and that the nondisclosure order prevented her from challenging the demand under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause.

"This lawsuit is not only about the faux authority granted to Smith through an unconstitutional appointment. It is also about ensuring that the Department of Justice—the very body responsible for enforcing federal law on behalf of our nation—acts only within its constitutional bounds," NCLA counsel L. Margaret Harker said in a statement.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The lawsuit seeks a declaration that Smith's appointment was unconstitutional, the return and destruction of Blackburn's phone records, and $1 in nominal damages. NCLA says the limited damages request reflects Blackburn's stated goal of obtaining judicial accountability for what the complaint alleges were constitutional violations committed while Smith exercised special counsel powers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Smith's counsel for comment.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Mamdani’s antisemitism plan draws criticism as rabbis say it avoids key driver of hate
summary: Three leading rabbis across Manhattan say they were never consulted on NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's antisemitism plan or how funding was allocated.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's declaration labeling Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a 'war criminal' has ignited widespread criticism. Prominent figures like former Ambassador Mike Huckabee and Danny Danon condemn Mamdani's remarks, accusing him of promoting antisemitism. This controversy unfolds as the Anti-Defamation League reports a staggering 480% increase in antisemitic incidents in New York City over the last decade, with 1,160 incidents in 2025 alone.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a multimillion-dollar strategy to combat antisemitism, drawing criticism from prominent Jewish leaders who described the announcement as an attempt to deflect attention from the mayor’s own rhetoric while avoiding one of the defining sources of modern anti-Jewish hostility: the demonization of Israel and Zionism.

Mamdani announced what his administration called the nation’s first municipal strategy dedicated to combating antisemitism, declaring that Jewish New Yorkers "should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America."

The mayor cited New York Police Department statistics showing that although Jewish residents constitute approximately 12% of the city’s population, antisemitic incidents account for more than half of its confirmed hate crimes.
EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN
"This is not only unacceptable, it’s something we all have an obligation to change," Mamdani said. "And City Hall will lead the way."

His administration said it is increasing hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, an increase of more than 800% from the previous year. The plan includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate violence and would restart an interagency security and infrastructure initiative disbanded in 2024.

The city also pledged $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture, alongside expanded education, reporting resources and security support for Jewish institutions.

The way that money would be distributed also drew scrutiny. Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, said that only $1 million is dedicated specifically to security while millions more would be directed through community initiatives.
MAMDANI IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER FIRST VETO DERAILS BIPARTISAN EFFORT TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM: 'DISAPPOINTED'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani inside 1 Police Plaza, New York, NY on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. (Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

"All of this money is pure pork barrel politics," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "Outside of a million dollars in security, it is all being spent on community initiatives that will reward his supporters."

The Jewish leaders who spoke with Fox News Digital welcomed the security investments but argued that physical protection alone cannot address an environment in which Jews increasingly feel pressured to distance themselves from Israel.

From Manhattan’s East Side to its West Side, three prominent rabbis shared another concern: Not one had been contacted by the mayor or his administration while the strategy was being developed, despite collectively leading some of the borough’s largest Jewish congregations.

Those concerns raise basic questions about how the strategy was constructed: which Jewish leaders and institutions helped shape it, how did the administration decide where the funding would go, and how were organizations selected to receive it? Fox News Digital asked those questions, along with Steinmetz’s criticism of the funding process, to the mayor’s office but had not received a response at the time of publication.

A Bronx man was charged with multiple hate crimes after allegedly disrupting Shabbat services and attacking a congregant and security member at Central Synagogue in Manhattan, police said. (REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz)

The mayor's strategy acknowledges rising antisemitism since Oct. 7 and expands Holocaust education, but does not directly address the hostility Jewish students have experienced on college campuses or examine when anti-Israel activism crosses into antisemitic harassment and intimidation. The three rabbis interviewed by Fox News Digital identified that omission as a significant weakness in the city’s strategy.

Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch, senior rabbi of Stephen Wise Free Synagogue in Manhattan and president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said the plan omits what he considers the central driver of contemporary antisemitism.
CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS
Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch criticized Mayor Mamdani, saying he is "evading the issue." (Shahar Azran)
"If the purpose here is to combat and reduce antisemitism, the plan omits the central driver of contemporary antisemitism, which is an obsessive loathing of Israel," Hirsch told Fox News Digital.

That hostility, he said, is directed "not only" toward the state of Israel but toward "the Zionist idea, the right of Israel to exist, the right of the Jewish people to self-determination in the land of Israel."

"To write a 30-page report and never mention the state of Israel, let alone address the vicious anti-Zionism, partially fomented by the mayor himself, is evading the issue," Hirsch said. "It’s not dealing head-on with the issue itself."
ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS
The NYPD said it is ramping up security at Jewish sites across New York City after Israel launched strikes on Iran overnight. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Hirsch welcomed the additional security funding, while emphasizing that Jewish institutions must routinely absorb expenses other communities do not face.
"The security obligations in every Jewish institution in the city are, in effect, an additional surtax on New York Jews that nobody else pays," he said. "And so any funds for security are welcome."
He also supported educational initiatives and Holocaust museum visits but said the city must teach more than the history of Jewish persecution.
"What I would like to see is a focus in New York public schools on the nexus, the connection between anti-Zionism and antisemitism," Hirsch said.

"One of the key lessons from the Holocaust," he added, is that "Jewish self-determination and Jewish empowerment are the answer to Jewish powerlessness that gave rise to centuries of antisemitism that culminated in genocide."

Thousands of anti-Israel protestors fill Freedom Plaza and the surrounding streets for rally and march calling for an end to the Israel - Hamas war, in Washington, DC on Saturday, November 4, 2023. (Rod Lamkey/CNP for Fox News Digital)
Steinmetz also said the mayor is using the strategy to avoid examining the consequences of his own language.
"Rather than taking responsibility for combating antisemitism, Mamdani is using this plan to deflect attention from himself," Steinmetz said. "His rhetoric has been reckless."
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER
Steinmetz said statistics measuring physical crimes capture only part of what Jewish New Yorkers experience.
"Far more common is the nasty look and whispered insult," he said. "You cannot talk about a trip to Israel at the water cooler. Jews feel like they have to hide parts of themselves to be accepted."

The mayor has long been an outspoken critic of the Israeli government and has faced scrutiny from Jewish leaders over his descriptions of Israel, Zionism and organizations that support the Jewish state. Critics argue that separating antisemitism from anti-Zionist rhetoric ignores how Jewish identity is experienced by much of the city’s Jewish population.

Anti-Israel agitators clash with NYPD at a 'Stop the Sale of Stolen Palestinian Land' protest against 'Great Israel Real Estate' event for Palestinian land sale at the Park East Synagogue in Manhattan on Tuesday, May 05, 2026, in New York City. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Rabbi Yosie Levine of The Jewish Center on Manhattan’s Upper West Side thanked the mayor for recognizing the severity of the problem but called for a corresponding change in his language.
"I want to thank the mayor for his commitment to combat antisemitism," Levine told Fox News Digital. "Acknowledging the problem is an important first step."
ISRAELI MEDICS TRAIN US SYNAGOGUES HOW TO RESPOND TO ATTACKS, AS HIGH HOLIDAYS APPROACH
"At the same time, we would welcome an equally clear commitment to stop using rhetoric that vilifies Jewish leaders and the Jewish state," Levine continued.
"When you turn Zionism into an accusation, you turn Zionists into the accused."
A spokesperson for the Jewish Federations of North America, referred Fox News Digital to a joint statement issued by UJA Federation of New York and the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York.

While the organizations recognized "positive elements" in the plan, including increased security funding and the expansion of established programs, they warned that it "fails to address a central issue that the mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers."
Anti-Israel activists protest outside the United Nations headquarters in New York, on April 7, 2025. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Those who truly seek to address antisemitism must unequivocally reject such rhetoric and help ensure that Jewish New Yorkers are never made to feel suspect, excluded or unsafe in their own city," the statement continued.
Mamdani said the administration’s efforts would ultimately benefit every community because "our safety is bound up together."
