HOW SWEEPSTAKES ENTRY DATA CAN REACH SCAMMERS
Marketing data can reveal who has responded to certain offers before, giving scammers another clue about who may be more likely to engage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What opportunity seeker lists actually mean

"Opportunity seeker" sounds like harmless marketing jargon. But in the Epsilon case, the Department of Justice (DOJ) showed how that label was being used inside a business unit that worked with fraudulent clients. According to Epsilon's deferred prosecution agreement, the company's clients included businesses sending deceptive solicitations involving sweepstakes, astrology, auto warranties, dietary supplements and government grants.

Epsilon employees called the people targeted by those offers "opportunity seekers" and referred to the clients sending them as "opportunistic." The court filing also says those opportunity seekers frequently came from the same group: older and vulnerable Americans.

Then there was the data behind the label. DOJ says Epsilon used transactional data and algorithms to identify "responsive buyers," or people most likely to respond to certain offers. Its database covered about 100 million U.S. households. Think about what that means. If you responded to one offer, that response could become a signal that you might respond to another. In the hands of a fraudster, that kind of information can make it much easier to decide who to target first.
This went far beyond one company

Epsilon eventually agreed to pay $150 million, including $22.5 million in criminal penalties and $127.5 million for victim compensation. Two former Epsilon employees, Robert Reger and David Lytle, were later convicted. A federal judge sentenced Reger to 10 years in prison and Lytle to four years.

According to the DOJ, they sold nearly 100 lists of names and addresses to one fraudulent client. That client used the information in a scheme that defrauded more than 218,000 people out of more than $23.7 million. Even more alarming, DOJ says more than 12,000 people were defrauded by that single scheme more than 20 times each.

Other cases followed. KBM Group entered a deferred prosecution agreement requiring a $33.5 million victim compensation payment and an $8.5 million criminal fine. DOJ says employees sold data tied to millions of Americans to more than a dozen clients they knew were engaged in fraudulent mass-mailing schemes.

Macromark, a Connecticut direct-mail services company, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. The company admitted that lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in losses. Wiland Inc. later entered a non-prosecution agreement with DOJ that included $4.4 million in victim compensation over data sold to operators of fraudulent schemes. By June 2025, DOJ said its Consumer Data Victim Compensation Fund had returned more than $129 million to more than 100,000 victims across the country.
A 2026 case shows this playbook is still alive

It would be easy to look at the earlier cases and think this was an old direct-mail problem. It wasn't. In May 2026, a federal judge sentenced Troy Murray of North Carolina to 121 months in prison after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

DOJ says Murray collected and sold lists containing names, phone numbers, home addresses and, in some cases, ages and email addresses of older Americans. His customers included people in Jamaica running lottery fraud schemes. And the scale was huge. From 2016 through 2023, DOJ says Murray sent scammers at least 22,000 lead lists containing information on more than 7 million older Americans.

Those lists typically sold for $500 for 100 to 300 names. DOJ says Murray made more than $5.2 million while victims lost more than $9.5 million. That is what makes these lists so valuable to scammers. They do not have to spend time figuring out who might pick up the phone or respond to an offer. Someone has already handed them a list of people to try first.
WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE
Federal cases show how lead lists containing names, addresses, phone numbers and other personal details have been sold to fraudsters targeting older Americans. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The same kind of targeting is still sold as marketing

These kinds of marketing lists are legal and can be used for legitimate advertising. Just because a list is for sale does not mean the company selling it or the company buying it is doing anything wrong. But the way some of these lists are described today sounds very familiar.

As of September 2026, Geon Media advertises a list called "Prime Opportunity Seekers - Buyers Only!" It includes 397,532 names and focuses on people who purchased business opportunities after responding to marketing campaigns. Marketers can narrow that list even further using details such as age, income, net worth and location. Geon also requires buyers to provide a sample mail piece.

NextMark advertises a list called "Sweeps Winners Only" made up of people who recently responded to sweepstakes offers. Its listing describes that audience as "highly impulsive" and promotes the list for sweepstakes, lotteries, credit cards and other offers.

Exact Data also advertises categories with names including "Sweepstakes Opportunity Purchasers" and "Gambling, Lottery, and Sweepstakes Enthusiasts." Its listings were updated in September 2026. None of that proves fraud. What it does show is how valuable your past behavior can be. Respond to the right kind of offer, and that response can become a data point that helps someone decide what to put in front of you next.
Why your response history can be so valuable

For a scammer, finding someone willing to respond can be half the battle. Calling or emailing random people takes time. A list of people who have already responded to certain offers gives them a much better place to start. That is what made Epsilon's data so valuable. DOJ says the company's algorithms could predict which people were most likely to respond to certain mailings. If you had responded before, that behavior could become another clue about what might get your attention next.

And there is a lot of money on the line. The FBI says people over 60 filed more than 201,000 complaints in 2025 and reported more than $7.7 billion in losses. The FBI does not say how many of those people were targeted through marketing or lead lists, so we cannot say those lists caused those losses. But the DOJ cases show something important: scammers have used targeted lists to help find people they believe are more likely to respond. That is why something as simple as entering a sweepstakes or responding to an offer can be more valuable than you might think. The response itself can become another piece of data about you.
Even everyday actions like entering a sweepstakes or responding to a promotion can become another data point used to decide which offers you may see next. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
6 steps to make yourself harder to target

You probably cannot find every private marketing database that contains your name. However, you can reduce the information available about you and become much more selective about what you hand over going forward.

Start with your full name. Then search your phone number and home address. Pay attention to people-search sites displaying your address, age, relatives, phone numbers or email addresses. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process. The FTC says you can request removal from people-search sites yourself for free, although you may need to repeat the process if your information appears again later.

A legitimate contest can still collect information for marketing. Before entering, read the privacy policy and official rules. Look for language explaining whether your information can be shared with advertisers or marketing partners. The FTC specifically warns that contest promoters may sell information to advertisers, which can lead to more targeted advertising, promotional mail, calls and spam.

If an entry form asks for information that seems unrelated to the promotion, stop and ask why it needs it. Avoid handing over extra details simply because a box appears on a form. Also watch for prechecked boxes giving permission for additional marketing. Every unnecessary piece of information you share gives a company one more data point that can potentially be added to your profile.

Consider creating an email address or alias used only for contests, loyalty programs and promotional offers. That keeps your primary email address out of some marketing databases and makes unexpected prize messages easier to spot. If someone contacts your main email account claiming you won a contest you entered with a different address, that alone should raise questions.

This one is simple. Real prizes are free. The FTC says anyone demanding taxes, processing fees, shipping charges or other payments before releasing a prize is running a scam. Also, never provide your bank account, credit card or Social Security number to claim a prize. If you are unsure whether an offer is real, find the company's official contact information yourself rather than calling a number in the letter, text or email.

If you sent money or personal information to a scammer, act quickly. Contact your bank or payment provider first if money changed hands. Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . If the scam came through the mail, you can also report it to the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. If someone used your personal information, IdentityTheft.gov can walk you through recovery steps. For anyone age 60 or older, the DOJ's National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11 (1-833-372-8311) offers free help Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern. DOJ says reporting certain financial losses quickly can improve the chances of recovering money, although recovery cannot be guaranteed.
What a personal data scan can and cannot tell you

There is no public search box that will show you every private marketing category attached to your name. A people-search or data-broker scan also cannot tell you whether your name appears on one of the specific "opportunity seeker" or criminal lead lists described above. And no data removal service can pull information back once criminals already have it.

What a scan can do is show you where personal details such as your name, address or phone number appear across covered people-search and data-broker sites. From there, you can start reducing that exposure. If the scan finds your information, you have two options. You can contact sites yourself and submit opt-out requests, or you can use a service that handles much of that work for you.

A data removal service can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of covered data brokers and people-search sites. Some plans also let you request removals from additional websites that fall outside the standard automated coverage.

It is worth knowing the limits too. Some private data-broker databases cannot be scanned directly. Instead, removal requests are sent to brokers that may hold your information. These services also cannot remove certain government records, court records or information already circulating in criminal databases.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

For me, the biggest takeaway here is that scammers do not always have to figure out who might respond. Sometimes, someone else has already done that work for them. The Epsilon case showed how marketing data and algorithms could identify people likely to respond to certain offers. DOJ says those "opportunity seekers" frequently included older and vulnerable Americans. And this problem has not been confined to old direct-mail cases. In 2026, a federal judge sentenced a man who DOJ says sold more than 22,000 lead lists containing information on over 7 million older Americans to lottery scammers. At the same time, legitimate marketers still sell highly specific lists based on things like sweepstakes responses and interest in business opportunities. That does not make those lists fraudulent. It does show just how much our past behavior can say about what we may respond to next. You may never know every list that has your name on it. But you can stop handing out unnecessary information, remove exposed personal data where possible and slow down whenever an unexpected offer lands in front of you.

Should companies be able to sell lists built around how likely someone is to respond to money-making or sweepstakes offers, especially when age and financial information can also be used for targeting? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: South Carolina mom accused of knife attack on young children; 6-year-old may lose arm: sheriff's office
summary: Taylor Gosnell allegedly stabbed her two children approximately 50 times in their South Carolina home before her 6-year-old called his grandmother.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A South Carolina boy’s call to his grandmother saying he was hungry led authorities to a home where investigators say his mother had stabbed him and his younger sibling dozens of times, leaving both children with severe injuries.

Taylor Gosnell, 35, is charged with two counts of attempted murder after allegedly attacking her children, ages 6 and 3, inside their Spartanburg County home during the overnight hours before they were discovered Saturday, according to authorities.
The 6-year-old called his grandmother Sept. 26, and told her his mother was not home and that he and his 3-year-old sibling were hungry, according to the Spartanburg County Sheriff’s Office.
ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY
Taylor Gosnell, 35, is charged with two counts of attempted murder and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime in Spartanburg County, S.C. (Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office)
The grandmother contacted a friend of Gosnell, and the two went to the residence. They found both children suffering from severe injuries and immediately dialed 911.
Deputies responding shortly after 2:30 p.m. found the residence in disarray, with numerous items damaged or broken, authorities said.

Investigators said the children suffered approximately 50 stab wounds between them, including injuries that penetrated to the bone. Both were initially taken to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center before being transferred to Prisma Health Children’s Hospital in Greenville, where they remained hospitalized and were expected to undergo additional surgeries.
SUBURBAN ILLINOIS BOY DIES IN SUSPECTED DOMESTIC HOMICIDE AS NEIGHBORS FEAR ANOTHER LINDSAY CLANCY CASE

Arrest warrants reviewed by Fox News Digital provide additional details about the alleged attack. The warrants allege Gosnell struck the children with a baseball bat and a circular knife, causing severe injuries, with intent to kill them.

Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still at the scene, according to the sheriff’s office. Deputies transported her to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center for an evaluation after observing behavior that raised concerns about her immediate well-being.
Authorities said Gosnell attempted to run from the ambulance before being transported and had to be restrained. She was medically cleared and released from the hospital shortly afterward.
DAYS AFTER LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL, ANOTHER MASSACHUSETTS MOM ACCUSED OF KILLING HER CHILDREN SEEKS FREEDOM
Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still at the scene. (Getty Images, File)
Investigators attempted to interview Gosnell, but no interview was conducted after she requested an attorney, according to the sheriff’s office.
Gosnell was booked into the Spartanburg County Detention Facility shortly before midnight Sept. 26, and was denied bond on both attempted murder charges.

Investigators later obtained two additional warrants charging Gosnell with possession of a weapon during a violent crime. Those warrants, also reviewed by Fox News Digital, allege she possessed the weapons during the attempted murders.
The children have been placed in protective custody and remain hospitalized, authorities said.
The investigation remains active and ongoing.

title: EXCLUSIVE: State Department revokes over 250,000 visas in broad immigration vetting crackdown
summary: The State Department has revoked over 250,000 visas under Trump for criminal activity, fraud, birth tourism and national security threats.
story: Tommy Pigott sat down at the White House with Fox News Digital to discuss the department's crackdown on visas, including birth tourism.

EXCLUSIVE: The State Department has revoked more than 250,000 visas since President Donald Trump took office, as the administration continues to crack down on unlawful immigration and increase vetting of who is allowed to visit the United States.

The revocations were for a variety of violations, including visa holders who violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against the U.S. or Americans, defrauded Americans, abused the immigration system, and endangered national security, a State Department official told Fox News Digital.

Among the visas revoked were 2,300 in connection with birth tourism, the practice of pregnant foreign nationals traveling to the U.S. specifically to give birth so their child automatically receives citizenship.
BIRTH TOURISM SCAMS DRAW SWEEPING CRACKDOWN AS VISA REVOCATIONS CLIMB

The Trump administration has been aggressive about revoking visas of foreign nationals, yanking thousands of visas of those who have committed a range of offenses and violated the terms of their stay in the United States, the State Department said. (Harry Hamburg/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the State Department has now revoked more than 250,000 visas — a historic milestone that reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting the American people," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said.

"Every visa decision is a national security decision. Through continuous vetting on a scale never seen before, we are identifying and removing those who commit crimes, support terrorism, defraud Americans, or abuse our immigration system," Pigott added. "A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right — and if you violate the terms of that privilege, you will lose it. We will not stop until every foreign national who threatens the safety of our communities is held accountable."

On Monday, the State Department revoked the visas of 27 Latin American officials, former officials, and their families over accusations of corruption. The officials are from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru.
Over the summer, the Trump administration began preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum in the U.S.
DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM
Over the summer, the Trump administration began preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 people. (iStock)

The effort would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to foreigners who later sought asylum. At the time, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said Americans were "fed up" with "bogus asylum claims."

"Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion,’" he wrote on X at the time.
TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS
The State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio has yanked thousands of visas for overstays and law violations — including support for terrorism. (Reuters)
He noted that frivolous claims have swamped the system, which could take years to adjudicate whether applicants are entitled to asylum in the U.S.

In August, the State Department also revoked more than 175,000 visas. The majority of those were revoked due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity, with assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug crimes being the leading causes.

A significant share of visas were revoked for reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement and other crimes, the agency said.

title: Penn State cocaine ring suspect’s attorney warns of ‘foolish’ move in alleged frat drug operation
summary: Five men accused in a cocaine distribution ring at Penn State indicated a plan to plead not guilty, with three requesting jury trials as the Centre County case advances.
story: A massive drug bust at Penn State is drawing attention to a dangerous new reality facing college campuses: party drugs are no longer just party drugs. Following the dismantling of a student-led dealing operation in State College, Centre County drug and alcohol specialist Cathy Arbogast speaks out on the surge of synthetic stimulants flooding rural communities across Pennsylvania.
Five men accused of being part of a cocaine distribution ring at Penn State filed court documents in Centre County, Pennsylvania, signaling plans to fight the charges against them.

Agostino Abbatiello, Mohammed Huraibi, Robert Zanolla, Thomas Robinson and Paul Robinson have each indicated they intend to plead not guilty as their cases move forward in Centre County court. The move comes despite testimony detailing kilogram-sized deals and a drug-packaging operation inside a fraternity house, though one of their attorneys warned it would be "foolish" to rush to judgment.

The Office of the Court Administrator said the five defendants waived their formal arraignments scheduled for Wednesday and will not appear at the Centre County Courthouse. Their next court appearance is scheduled for Nov. 16 for a pretrial conference.
PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE RING SUSPECTS ALLEGEDLY USED CASH APP, SNAPCHAT TO ARRANGE DRUG DEALS

Abbatiello, Zanolla and Thomas Robinson requested jury trials on their waiver forms. Huraibi and Paul Robinson indicated they intend to plead not guilty but did not select either a jury or non-jury trial.

Agostino Abbatiello arrives at Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pa., on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Abbatiello is accused of masterminding a cocaine ring at Penn State University. (Kamil Krzaczynski for Fox News Digital)

Thomas Robinson, a former Delta Upsilon fraternity member, testified that he and Huraibi began buying cocaine from Abbatiello in 2023, starting with about 100 grams for roughly $4,000.
Robinson said the cocaine was stored in his fraternity room, where he and Huraibi broke it into half-gram bags and sold them for about $80 each.

The quantities later grew to kilogram-sized purchases, Robinson testified. He said he eventually began buying directly from Abbatiello through Snapchat, where messages disappeared after 24 hours.
Huraibi also testified that he and Robinson bought cocaine in bulk to resell, initially packaging the drugs themselves before fraternity pledges became involved.

Robert Zanolla, 24, is accused of helping transport cocaine from New York City to State College, Pennsylvania. (Pennsylvania Office of the Attorney General Dave Sunday)

Charging documents portray Abbatiello as a top-level supplier who allegedly used fraternity connections to distribute cocaine near Penn State. Zanolla is accused of helping make trips to New York to obtain cocaine and transport it back to the State College area.

title: Teen killer avoids state’s first female execution in over 200 years – for now
summary: Christa Pike's execution was halted by a Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals stay in a 2-1 split decision, leaving Tennessee's death penalty case unresolved.
story: The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's request for an all-female execution squad and execution by hanging instead of lethal injection, citing childhood trauma involving men.

Convicted Tennessee killer Christa Pike has been spared at the last minute from becoming the first woman executed in the state since the early 1800s after the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals issued a stay Wednesday morning.
In a 2-1 split decision, the court issued a stay "until further notice" as the court weighs motions filed by Pike's attorneys and the Tennessee Attorney General's Office.
The state immediately appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, seeking to have the stay lifted.

Pike, 50, was 18 in 1995 when she, her boyfriend and another person beat, kicked and stabbed their 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer to death in a brutal "satanic" attack that Pike claimed took between 30 minutes and an hour, according to court documents.
MULTIPLE DEATH SENTENCES IN DIFFERENT STATES ARE SET TO BE CARRIED OUT WITHIN 24 HOURS: 'NOT VERY COMMON'
An undated portrait photograph of Colleen Slemmer provided by her mother. (May Martinez/Special to the News Sentinel)
Pike and Slemmer knew each other through a vocational program in Knoxville called the Job Corps Center, the documents state.

Pike had accused Slemmer of "trying to get [her] boyfriend" and "running her mouth," the case file shows. A day before the killing, she told another classmate she wanted to kill Slemmer because she "just felt mean that day," according to the records. She was armed with a box cutter and a meat cleaver.
Pike and her accomplices lured Slemmer out, telling her they wanted to go to a music store and pick up some marijuana they'd hidden in a park nearby.
Pike attacked her, knocked her to the ground and hit her in the face with her knee and foot, according to court documents.

At trial, forensic psychiatrist Dr. William Bernet testified that the crime had "satanic elements" but also appeared to involve "the phenomenon of collective aggression, in which a group of people become emotionally aroused and 'the end result is that they engage in some kind of violent, extremely violent activity,'" court records show.

Dr. Eric Engum testified that Pike had been diagnosed with "very severe borderline personality disorder" in addition to showing signs of cannabis dependence and depression. However, he said, she had no symptoms of brain damage or insanity.

Neither Shipp nor the third attacker, Shadolla Peterson, received death sentences. Shipp was under 18 at the time and not eligible for capital punishment. Peterson testified for the state.

title: Florida judge rips into mom accused of leaving 4 children at home to go on 3-day cruise
summary: Bodycam footage showed four children hiding in a bathroom after Nathalie Belizaire allegedly left them alone to board the Carnival Conquest.
story: Bodycam footage captures the moment police found four unattended children —including a 2-month-old infant — hiding in a bathroom, while a judge fires back at defense claims in court. (WSVN)
A Florida mother is facing four felony charges after allegedly abandoning her four young children — including a 2-month-old infant — to take a three-day vacation on a cruise ship to the Bahamas.

Nathalie Belizaire, 29, was charged with four counts of child neglect after she boarded Carnival Cruise Line’s Carnival Conquest, leaving her children unattended in her North Miami Beach residence. Police said U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers took her into custody Monday as she disembarked.
"You cannot make this up," Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mindy Glazer said in Tuesday court footage. "We are just grateful nothing worse happened to those kids.
MOTHER, BOYFRIEND ALLEGEDLY ABANDONED BLINDFOLDED YOUNG SONS IN REMOTE FOREST AS PART OF 'GAME': REPORTS
Nathalie Belizaire, 29, bows her head after using her orange jail attire to wipe away a tear during an arraignment Tuesday. (WSVN)
"Who leaves four little kids alone to go on a cruise?
"The poor kids were home alone."

The children were discovered by police Saturday, the day after the ship set sail. Bodycam footage showed four kids coming out of hiding in a bathroom – a 2-year-old toddler, a pre-teen and what appeared to be a teenage girl holding a newborn baby.
Lether Bazile, the father of the 2-month-old, told police that Belizaire claimed she was leaving the children with their great-grandmother, the New York Post reported.
BABYSITTER ACCUSED OF KIDNAPPING TWO YOUNG SISTERS WAS PREVIOUSLY CHARGED WITH ABDUCTING NEWBORN

A toddler comes to the door of a bathroom after North Miami Beach Police were called to an apartment to find four children allegedly abandoned by their mother, who left for a three-day weekend cruise to the Bahamas. (WSVN)
The father was tipped off by the mother's absence by Belizaire’s WhatsApp story two days earlier that appeared to show a Carnival Cruise Line ticket, he told police.
When Bazile stopped by Belizaire's home, he saw the television glowing through the blinds and heard the children's voices inside.
He immediately called the police, who entered the home and found the four children hiding in a bathroom with no adult present.

According to authorities, the children's grandmother, Denise Wilkes, told officers that Belizaire had promised to drop the kids off but never showed up. Furthermore, Belizaire’s brother, Steven Borgella, informed police that his sister had texted him at 8 p.m. ET on the day the children were found, asking him to check in on them.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH ABUSING HER KIDS, SETTING FIRE IN HOUSE WHILE MAKING MENTAL HEALTH DEFENSE

Footage showed a 2-year-old toddler, a pre-teen and a teen carrying a newborn baby leaving an apartment in North Miami Beach after allegedly being abandoned by their mother for a three-day weekend cruise. (WSVN)
Belizaire was arrested Monday as she disembarked the vessel at the port in Miami. She declined to speak to officers.
During the Tuesday hearing, Belizaire’s defense attorney argued that her abandoning the children to go on vacation was "just an allegation at this time," noting that she denies the claims.
"At this time, it is only an allegation; she denies the allegation," the defense attorney said.
"Of course she does," Glazer said as the accused showed exasperation.
"They arrested her disembarking from the cruise ship!" the judge then shot back.
TWO MISSING CHILDREN RESCUED FROM TRAILER AS POLICE ARREST BABYSITTER ON KIDNAPPING CHARGES
"I understand that, judge, I understand that," the attorney replied. "The question is who was the one responsible for the children at the time?"
Glazer thought for a second, before saying, "usually it's the mother, the person that gave birth to them."

"There are also others responsible, it's not just mothers," the defense attorney replied. "It's not just mothers that are in charge of children, judge. It's also fathers and grandparents and other people."
"See, the mothers always know who their children are," Glazer said. "Fathers may not know, but it looks like different fathers here. One of the fathers grew concerned and called the police."

Belizaire was given a stay away order until the Department of Children and Families can investigate. She faces four felony counts of child neglect without great bodily harm. Bond was set at $10,000, $2,500 per child.

This recent arrest is not Belizaire's first run-in with the law. She previously faced aggravated battery charges in January 2025 after allegedly pepper-spraying a neighbor in the face during a dispute regarding her daughter, the Post reported.

title: Ole Miss students' toxicology reports will be done 'in due course,' families to be notified first: officials
summary: Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang were found dead with Smax synthetic kratom tablets near them, officials said.
story: Madison Scarpino reports on the deaths of two University of Mississippi students and the subsequent warnings issued about kratom-like substances found at the scene.
The toxicology reports for two Ole Miss students who died on Sept. 21 will be completed "in due course," with the families being notified of results first, an official tells Fox News Digital.

Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead on Sept. 21, both with similar packages of kratom or synthetic kratom found to be in their possession, according to the court documents. Officials detailed that Hamilton "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema," which would be consistent with a drug overdose. Strang was found "cold to the touch" when first responders arrived at his house near campus.

Alex Gibert, press secretary for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, told Fox News Digital: "Commissioner met with the [medical examiner's] Office yesterday and we expect the reports to be finalized ‘in due course.’ The families will be the first to know."

The news comes as the American Kratom Association hosted a news conference on Wednesday, criticizing the "delay in publicly identifying the specific products purchased by two Ole Miss students before their deaths."
The group says these tablets "are not natural kratom leaf and that students should have been specifically warned about these products under investigation."
VAPE STORE CLERK NEAR OLE MISS CAMPUS WARNED BUYER 'PEOPLE WERE DYING' FROM KRATOM PILLS, AFFIDAVIT SAYS
Robert Strang and Aidan Hamilton in a split image provided by their families. (Strang family, Kathleen Hamilton/Facebook)

Packaging on the kratom items found near both men were labeled "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets, which is a "Kratom like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops" that people buy for the "narcotic like effect," according to the court documents.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Hamilton made several purchases in September at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where workers Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested and face a charge of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute. Officials did not say in the court documents that the kratom found near him when he died came from that store. One of the purchases was made one day before Hamilton was found dead.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Packages of synthetic kratom products, including Smax Pseudo-DHM and Smax Pseudo tablets, that authorities say were found at the scene where Robert Strang was discovered dead. (Court records)

One hour after finding Hamilton dead, police were dispatched to a house near campus and found Strang dead. A package of the "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets was found on his nightstand, along with 20 to 30 nitrous oxide cans, known as "whippets," which Strang's roommates said he used daily. Strang's roommates told officers that he was watching football and took a Xanax bar the day before being found dead.

Officials said the synthetic kratom-derived product Strang had bought was purchased at a gas station about 30 minutes away from Oxford.

Stewart Hall, a dorm building on the University of Mississippi campus where an 18-year-old student is believed to have died on Monday. Dispatch records show first responders arrived within a minute of being sent to the address. (Adam Sabes/Fox News Digital)

title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer raises explosive doubt over who killed her children
summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington argued for the first time that prosecutors failed to prove she killed her three children.
story: Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani breaks down Kevin Reddington’s new reasonable-doubt argument — a potential shift from Clancy’s mental illness defense.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer made a surprise shift in strategy Tuesday, according to legal analysts — shifting gears from his argument at trial that she was not criminally responsible because she suffered from postpartum psychosis.
"Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday. "Where is the evidence she did this?"
Reddington made the argument while asking Sullivan to enter a not guilty finding after the jury deadlocked.
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ASKS FOR ONE THING IN NEW VIDEO AFTER MISTRIAL DRAMA

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day. The Lindsay Clancy jury resumes deliberations for a sixth day on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)
"I submit to the court there is no evidence she made any statements, as far as the actual killing of the children, which forms the basis of the indictments," Reddington said.
Plymouth County prosecutors countered, calling his assertion "a laughable argument." But it marked a striking change in the way he's argued the case in the past.
He pointed to what he described as gaps in the physical evidence, including the blood, DNA, timing and circumstances surrounding Clancy’s suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed.
LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE

"For the first time, we saw Kevin Reddington say that there’s reasonable doubt as to whether Lindsay Clancy actually killed her children," said former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani, who has been closely following the case. "He's never said that in the courtroom, outside the courtroom — and in fact at the beginning of the first trial, he offered to stipulate to Lindsay killing her three children."
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a verdict following roughly a week of deliberations. Since then, several jurors have spoken out publicly, describing an 11-1 deadlock with only one man voting to find her guilty of murder.
LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS

The 11 sided with Reddington's not guilty due to mental illness or defect defense. He argued that Clancy was not criminally responsible for strangling her children with exercise bands due to postpartum psychosis.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin J. Reddington, addresses the media outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, August 26, 2026. Clancy is on trial for the murder of her three children in January 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Only one juror voted to convict, and Reddington started calling him an "obstructionist" — first last week when approached by Fox News Digital and again outside the courthouse Tuesday. During the hearing, Reddington also raised concerns about the prosecution’s case and the police investigation launched after Clancy was found in the backyard suffering from injuries that left her paralyzed.
LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN
Lindsay Clancy is pictured at the Plymouth County Superior Court. (Pool)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"This may just be a defense lawyer denying everything, using the kitchen sink approach, hoping one of these arguments would resonate with Judge Sullivan," Rahmani said. "Or it could be a shift in defense strategy, where maybe instead of arguing insanity or lack of criminal responsibility at the retrial, they put on a third party culpability defense as well, arguing that maybe someone else is the real killer."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Jennifer Sprague entered a bag of prescription pills that were prescribed to Lindsay Clancy into evidence during the first day of her trial. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Reddington's comments came during oral arguments on what's called a Rule 25(b)(2) motion — asking Sullivan to override the deadlocked jury and enter a not-guilty finding on the alleged grounds that the Commonwealth's evidence was legally insufficient to garner a conviction.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT
Such motions are routine but seldom successful, according to Carol Erskine, a retired Massachusetts judge and child welfare advocate who has been following the case closely.
LINDSAY CLANCY DA RARELY DOES PLEA DEALS, BUT HER CASE COULD BE THE 'EXCEPTION,' VETERAN ATTORNEY SAYS

Lindsay Clancy listens to her attorney Kevin Reddington cross-examine a witness about her cellphone during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)
GOT A TIP?

"He is arguing that [they] did not prove each and every element as required by law," she told Fox News Digital. "I understand why people don’t get this, but he had to argue sufficiency of evidence under Rule 25(b)(2) case law. He told the judge he asked for a Bowden instruction and was denied, which meant he was challenging the poor investigation/search at the home by police. It’s a very nuanced argument."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
It's also a different argument than the prior Rule 25 motion that Reddington filed at the end of Clancy's mistrial, which Sullivan denied.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
"I will say it was a total surprise that his strategy changed from the original 25(b)(2) motion," Erskine said. "Did not expect it."
LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW
Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2 for another motion hearing. She has pending motions to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds and to open an inquiry into the holdout juror.

A new trial has not yet been scheduled. Both the prosecution and the defense told the court they needed more time, and Reddington said that he's not available to start one until June 2027.

title: Ohio cancer patient sues hospital after surgeon allegedly amputated wrong leg
summary: An Ohio woman is now a double amputee after her surgeon allegedly chopped off the wrong leg when she underwent a required amputation procedure.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An Ohio woman is suing after her surgeon allegedly amputated the wrong leg when she underwent a below-the-knee amputation that the lawsuit says was required because of cancer in her right leg.

Sharon Jacks, who is now a double amputee, was scheduled to have a below-the-knee amputation of her right leg at Selby General Hospital in Marietta, Ohio, on Sept. 19, 2025, but she woke up to her left leg missing, according to the lawsuit, WBNS reported.
"She went into surgery, and when she woke up, the wrong leg had been taken off," Jacks’ attorney Brad Layne told the outlet. "It defies explanation, obviously."
The leg that was originally supposed to be amputated was later cut off as well, leaving her without either leg.
FLORIDA DOCTOR CHARGED AFTER ALLEGEDLY REMOVING WRONG ORGAN DURING SURGERY
Sharon Jacks was scheduled to have a below-the-knee amputation of her right leg at Selby General Hospital, but she woke up to her left leg missing. (Google Maps)
Jacks' lawsuit names the hospital, her surgeon and other members of the surgical team, accusing them of "a complete failure of basic safety procedures."
Layne said in a press release that "there is simply no excuse" for what happened, adding that "complete and total failure by multiple medical professionals caused this catastrophe."

"Despite several opportunities to identify the mistake and stop the procedure, the surgical team somehow never noticed they were operating on the wrong leg," he said. "Now every day for the rest of her life, Sharon Jacks must live with the consequences of those failures."
According to Jacks' attorney, medical records he reviewed indicate the surgeon initially marked the correct leg, but the wrong leg was still amputated.
"The mark was still on the correct leg after the wrong leg had been taken off," Layne said.

According to the complaint, the medical team had two surgical "time-outs" before Jacks’ procedure. The lawsuit notes that "time-outs" are conducted to confirm the patient’s identity, the planned operation and the correct surgical location before an incision is made.
The lawsuit names the hospital, the surgeon and other members of the surgical team, accusing them of "a complete failure of basic safety procedures." (iStock)

"Every person in that operating room is responsible to make sure that that is verified before moving forward, and that includes the doctor, the staff, the nurses, the anesthesiologist, everybody that’s involved," Layne said.
"The records say that happened twice, but somehow Ms. Jacks is missing a leg that should have not been removed," he added.

Surgery on the wrong place is viewed as one of the most serious preventable medical errors and is often referred to as a "never event," a term that is recognized in the healthcare industry, the lawsuit claims.
"It shouldn’t happen in any type of medicine. It shouldn’t happen anywhere. It shouldn’t happen in a veterinary setting, even," Layne said.

The lawsuit seeks compensatory and punitive damages for Jacks to cover previous and future medical expenses, pain and suffering, emotional distress, permanent impairment and loss of enjoyment of life.
WOMAN WINS MASSIVE SETTLEMENT AFTER BLADDER MISTAKENLY REMOVED DURING SURGERY FOR BENIGN CYST

The lawsuit seeks compensatory and punitive damages for Sharon Jacks to cover previous and future medical expenses, pain and suffering, emotional distress, permanent impairment and loss of enjoyment of life. (Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Selby General Hospital confirmed an "adverse surgical event" happened in September 2025, saying the surgical team "responded immediately to address the medical needs of the patient involved and provide support to their family."

"Our proactive review of what took place confirmed this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed. Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions," the hospital said in a statement to WBNS.

The hospital said it has fully cooperated with a review by the Ohio Department of Health, saying the review confirmed its surgical protocols are "safe and effective" and that its clinical and leadership teams "have implemented corrective measures across our organization to prevent a situation like this from recurring.
"We are saddened by what occurred, and our team continues to keep this patient and their family in our prayers," the statement reads.

title: Utah man released after decades on death row as DNA evidence excludes him from 1985 killing
summary: A Utah man who spent decades on death row was released on bail after DNA evidence excluded him from the 1985 killing of a police chief's aunt.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Utah man who has spent decades on death row after he was convicted of killing a police chief's aunt has been released after prosecutors said newly analyzed DNA evidence excluded him as the source of DNA recovered from key pieces of evidence in the case.

Douglas Stewart Carter, 71, was let out on bail late Monday over objections from the victim's family. He must wear a GPS monitor while he awaits a new trial in the killing of Eva Olesen, who was found tied up, stabbed and shot inside her Provo home on Feb. 27, 1985, during what investigators suspected was a robbery.
A judge ordered him not to have any contact with Olesen's family.
The Utah Supreme Court ordered a new trial last year, pointing to misconduct by investigators.
MAN ‘FRAMED’ IN ‘SATANIC’ MURDER FREED AFTER 22 YEARS WINS $24M AS REAL KILLER STILL UNKNOWN

Douglas Stewart Carter, front left, and his son Tyler Anger, right, walk out of the Utah County Jail after a Utah judge ordered Carter's release from jail on Monday Sept. 28, 2026, in Spanish Fork, Utah. (AP Photo/George Frey)
Carter has maintained his innocence and argues that he was coerced into a signed confession.

No physical evidence linked Carter to the crime scene, but the jury convicted him based on the confession and the testimony of two witnesses who claimed he bragged about killing Olesen, although those witnesses later recanted.
A DNA analysis received on Sept. 22 excluded Carter as a possible match to blood found on a doorknob and genetic material recovered from the handle of a knife used to stab Olesen.
Judge Derek Pullan said those findings further undermined the case against Carter but noted that a jury could still say that he killed Olesen.
"This is going to be a lot for him," Carter's son, Tyler Anger, said on Monday as he waited for his father after his release was ordered.

Carter will be placed in an extended-stay hotel located near Anger, who was adopted by another family as an infant and did not learn about his father's conviction until years later, according to Carter's attorney, Neal Hamilton.
Carter will need therapy to deal with his extended incarceration, Hamilton said.
"If the state of Utah had their way, he would have been executed 15, 20 years ago before we discovered the misconduct," Hamilton said.
Hamilton also urged prosecutors to seek dismissal of an aggravated murder charge still pending against Carter.
NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ADAM MONTGOMERY'S MURDER CONVICTION IN DAUGHTER HARMONY'S DEATH

Douglas Stewart Carter sits in a car after he was released from the Utah County Jail as a Utah judge ordered his release from jail on Monday Sept. 28, 2026, in Spanish Fork, Utah. (AP Photo/George Frey)
A two-month retrial was planned next year, but county prosecutors withdrew a notice last week that they wanted to pursue the death penalty.
Utah County prosecutor Erwin Petilos told the judge on Monday that reassessing Carter's bail was "necessary and fair" as the state continues to examine the remaining evidence in the case.
Carter was living with his mother in Utah when Olesen was killed.

By April 1985, Carter had fled Utah, believing he was a suspect in an unrelated assault case, court documents show. He was detained two months later in Nashville, where he signed a confession while under interrogation by a Provo detective.
Carter said later that his confession was coerced, saying he falsely admitted to the crime after police repeatedly threatened him.

He was convicted and sentenced to death after a trial in which the defense called no witnesses to testify. Carter was sentenced to death again after a 1992 retrial, and courts in Utah later denied multiple appeals from Carter's legal team.

In 2011, the two witnesses from Carter's original trial were tracked down in Mexico, admitting they had been told to lie in court and had received cash and gifts from police in exchange for their testimonies. They said police told them not to disclose the payments and that police and prosecutors threatened them and their son with deportation if they did not implicate Carter in the killing.

More than a decade of legal fights ensued before the Utah Supreme Court stepped in last year and ordered a new trial, citing "multiple instances of intentional misconduct" by police and a prosecutor. A DNA analysis of the evidence was conducted in response to that order, and prosecutors said the results arrived last week, which excluded Carter from the crime.
Prosecutors declined to say whether they will use the DNA evidence to search for other suspects with matching DNA.

Attorneys for Carter, who is Black, have said witnesses saw a White man fleeing the crime scene and that an investigator suppressed evidence that could implicate other suspects, including the victim’s husband, Orla Olesen.
Former death row inmate Douglas Stewart Carter appears in 4th District Court in Provo, Utah, for a bond hearing on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Rick Egan/The Salt Lake Tribune via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Prosecutors were close to filing charges against the husband, but a Provo police lieutenant urged them not to so he could continue investigating, according to the defense attorneys. Carter was then identified as a suspect, according to court documents.
Orla Olesen, who died in 2009, told police he found his wife dead in their home, partially undressed and with her hands tied behind her back.
Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of Eva Olesen, said during the bond hearing on Monday that her family had "serious concerns" about Carter's release.
"By golly we were hoping for a concrete match," Olesen said of the DNA analysis. "It doesn't mean he wasn't there."
"We just want justice for Eva. And if he had any part of it we want that to be known," she added.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Venezuelan national shot by ICE officer in Austin charged with assaulting federal officer
summary: The Justice Department charged Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez with assaulting a federal officer after an Austin vehicle pursuit ended in an ICE shooting.
story: The footage appears to show authorities chasing Wilber Rafael Garces Perez just before he was shot (Credit: X @Savsays via X).

A Venezuelan national who was shot by an ICE officer following a vehicle pursuit in Austin earlier this month has been charged with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer, the Justice Department announced Tuesday.

Federal prosecutors allege that Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, refused ICE officers' commands to exit his vehicle during a targeted traffic stop before speeding away and striking one officer in the torso with his driver's side-view mirror.
Garces-Perez faces up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted, according to DOJ.

According to the complaint, officers first spotted Garces-Perez's vehicle outside a restaurant, ran its license plate and confirmed that an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal against him before initiating the stop.
AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION
A federal complaint states that one ICE officer turned off his body camera during a vehicle pursuit that later ended with a second officer shooting Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez. (Department of Justice)

The accounts differ over whether the vehicles made contact as officers stopped Garces-Perez. The officer told investigators there was no contact between the vehicles, while Garces-Perez claimed the ICE SUV's maneuver caused a collision before the officers approached him.
During the encounter, Garces-Perez provided officers with his driver's license, according to the complaint.

The officers described the initial encounter as "pleasant and not aggressive," according to the complaint. After officers instructed Garces-Perez to place the vehicle in park and step out, body camera footage shows him abruptly closing his window and driving away, according to the complaint.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET
Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, was shot as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were trying to take him into custody in Austin, Texas. (Austin Police Department)

Garces-Perez later told federal investigators that he disregarded the officers' command to exit the vehicle and drove away, according to the complaint. The complaint states that he was read his Miranda rights in Spanish, said he understood them and agreed to speak with investigators without an attorney present.
As he drove away, Garces-Perez's driver's side-view mirror struck one of the officers in the torso, according to the complaint.
According to the complaint, ICE officers pursued Garces-Perez through commercial and residential areas with emergency lights and sirens activated.

The officer wearing a body camera lost sight of both Garces-Perez and the second ICE officer while requesting assistance from a DPS dispatcher and then turned off his camera, according to the complaint. The second officer, who later fired his weapon, was not equipped with a body camera.
DEM REACTIONS WITHIN MOMENTS OF AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARK VIRAL OUTRAGE LOCALLY, ONLINE: 'DISQUALIFYING'

Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, was charged with assaulting, resisting, interfering with and impeding a federal officer following an ICE vehicle pursuit in Austin, Texas, according to the Justice Department. (Wilber Garces / Facebook)
The second officer later called his partner and reported that Garces-Perez had attempted to strike him with his vehicle, prompting the officer to fire his service weapon, according to the complaint.

Garces-Perez was struck by a bullet in his upper back, according to the complaint. He told investigators that the officer's SUV rammed his vehicle to force it into a spinout and that, after he was shot, the officer opened his driver's door, removed the keys from the ignition and told him to remain inside while an ambulance was en route.
Garces-Perez's immigration case has also been the subject of competing claims.

Fox News previously reported that his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said the order was issued after a hearing notice was sent to an old address despite Garces-Perez having updated his address with the court.
TRUMP REVIVES SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION SHOWDOWN AFTER HOCHUL PARDON TORPEDOED FIRST CASE
Federal prosecutors allege Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez fled a targeted ICE traffic stop in Austin before his vehicle's side mirror struck an officer in the torso. (Department of Justice)
ICE has disputed claims surrounding his immigration status, saying his work authorization expired in 2025 and that a work permit does not itself confer lawful immigration status.
His attorney has said Garces-Perez remains seriously ill and has a bullet lodged in his body while being held at an ICE detention facility.
Lincoln-Goldfinch, responding to the criminal complaint in a social media post, called for DHS to release the body camera footage.

"The criminal complaint also provides another critical piece of information: one of the officers involved in the incident had a body camera that was turned off at some point during the pursuit. We have not seen that footage. DHS must release the body camera footage immediately and provide full transparency to the American public," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote.

"He is now facing proceedings in both a federal criminal case and his federal immigration habeas case. We are working through what these developments mean, and we will share additional information as we are able."
DOJ said Garces-Perez made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday.

A detention hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2.

summary: Emonnie Branch was on probation for securities fraud and wanted for a violation before the traffic stop that left Trooper Hayden Phillips dead.
story: Kentucky officials mourn Trooper Hayden Phillips, a husband and father of three, and vow justice after his killing during a traffic stop.
The Tennessee man accused of killing a Kentucky state trooper was on probation and already wanted for a violation, with a criminal record that included assault, fraud and illegally possessing a gun.

CALIFORNIA GUNMAN REPEATEDLY RELEASED BEFORE DEADLY RAMPAGE, FIERY SHOOTOUT WITH DEPUTIES
Emonnie Branch, 51, is being held without bond in the killing of Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips. (Warren County Detention Center)
"Looks like he has a very extensive and varied criminal history," Commonwealth’s Attorney Kori Bumgarner said during Tuesday’s arraignment, the outlet reported.
CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND
Emonnie Branch was on probation when he was accused of killing Trooper Hayden Phillips, Tennessee correction records show. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

Dean said Branch’s prior convictions included attempted domestic assault, violating a no-contact order and securities fraud. Court records reviewed by the outlet also showed a 2009 conviction for illegally possessing a firearm as a convicted felon.

Fox 17 reported that Branch was arrested twice this year for probation violations. Warren County Regional Jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital show he is being held without bond on the murder charge and a fugitive charge.
SUSPECTS AT LARGE AFTER TUCSON POLICE RECRUIT KILLED, PIMA COUNTY CORRECTIONS OFFICER WOUNDED IN SHOOTING
Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips was killed while patrolling Interstate 65 in Warren County on Monday. (KY State Police)

Phillips was shot and killed during a traffic stop on Interstate 65 in Warren County Monday, Kentucky State Police said. Authorities identified Branch as the suspect and issued a statewide Blue Alert before Louisville Metro Police captured him that evening.

"He was senselessly murdered," U.S. Attorney Kyle Bumgarner said Monday night during a news briefing. "We have a wife that expected her husband to come home. We have three little boys who don’t have a dad."
JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER
Kentucky State Police released an image of a Honda Civic they said was present during the shooting of Trooper Hayden Phillips on Interstate 65. (KY State Police)

He pledged that the Justice Department would give state prosecutors and investigators "every tool" and "every bit of support" it could to help them pursue the maximum sentence.
Kentucky State Police Commissioner Col. Phillip Burnett Jr. condemned the suspect’s "cowardly actions" and explained why he had mentioned his name only once.
"I want you to know I only mentioned his name one time," Burnett said.

"I’ve laid here all night waiting for him to come home… for the radio to click off, the gun belt to hang," she wrote on Facebook.
"I promise to pick up all the pieces and force myself to carry on for your boys. I know you would want me to," she added.
State police escorted Phillips’ body to Glasgow Tuesday. A candlelight vigil is scheduled for Thursday at 6:30 p.m. local time.

"Trooper Hayden Phillips was a hero who sacrificed everything protecting our people and our commonwealth, and it is our sacred duty to honor him and his family," Beshear said.
He urged Kentuckians to pray for Jordan and their three children and encouraged donations to the Kentucky State Police Foundation, saying all proceeds would go directly to the family.

title: Suspect accused of killing Pittsburgh pediatrician sexually assaulted woman hours earlier: police
summary: Elijah Hemingway allegedly sexually assaulted a woman in Wilkinsburg before entering a nearby home and fatally stabbing a Pittsburgh pediatrician.
story: Retired pretrial investigator Kelly Rae Robertson argues that no-cash bail policies are being shaped by financial incentives on ‘America’s Newsroom.’
The suspect accused of killing a Pittsburgh pediatrician and critically injuring his wife during a midnight home invasion allegedly sexually assaulted a separate woman in public just hours earlier.

Elijah Hemingway, 32, allegedly ambushed the woman Wednesday morning as she was walking along a path that connects to an alley in Wilkinsburg, the Allegheny County Police Department said in a Facebook post Saturday.
Officials alleged Hemingway then stole the woman's cell phone during the incident.
Authorities said the victim did not know Hemingway before the alleged assault.
PITTSBURGH DOCTOR STABBED TO DEATH AFTER INTRUDER ALLEGEDLY ATTACKS HIM, WIFE AS THEY SLEPT: POLICE
First responders load Elijah Hemingway into an ambulance after his arrest in the home invasion murder of Pittsburgh Dr. Idris Evans Sept. 24, 2026. (KDKA)
Wilkinsburg police then notified Allegheny County detectives, who further investigated the alleged sexual assault alongside the homicide case.

Detectives recovered "multiple items connecting Hemingway to the reported sexual assault, along with the victim's cell phone that was reported stolen during the incident," Allegheny County police said.
After a consultation with the district attorney's office, county police said they filed additional charges against Hemingway, including rape, sexual assault and robbery.
BELOVED TEACHER KILLED AS SHE SLEPT, DAUGHTER STABBED IN ATTACK AS MOTIVE REMAINS UNCLEAR: DA
Dr. Idris Evans was the medical director of the Pediatric Critical Care Transport Team at UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh. (UPMC)
The Wilkinsburg attack happened just outside Edgewood, Pennsylvania, where Hemingway allegedly entered a home and stabbed a couple just hours later while they were sleeping early Thursday morning.
The pediatrician killed in the attack was identified as Dr. Idris Evans, 46, who was pronounced dead after first responders rushed him to a hospital.
According to a police report, Hemingway attacked the couple while in his underwear. Evans' wife told police that he appeared "psychotic" and claimed to be "God" during the incident.
As the couple fought back, Evans' wife yelled for their children, ages 8 and 12, to get out of the house, according to the police report.

She also told investigators that Evans called the attacker "Elijah," as though he knew him, according to the police report. However, county authorities told KDKA they could not confirm whether Evans and Hemingway had any preexisting relationship.
Evans' wife told police she did not know the suspect and was unsure how he entered their home.
CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND

The Evans family pictured in an undated photograph from a GoFundMe campaign launched for their benefit. Dr. Idris Evans, far right, was killed in a home invasion stabbing early Thursday morning. His wife, center, was hospitalized in stable condition. (GoFundMe)
During the investigation, police said Hemingway gave an account of the night that did not align with their findings.

Hemingway claimed Evans had invited him back to the home hours earlier and allowed him inside, according to the police report. He also accused Evans of attacking him with a knife and said he sustained a stab wound to his back, the report said.
However, authorities said they found no stab wound on Hemingway's back and could not locate a bicycle he claimed to have used to get to the home.
Authorities brought seven charges against Hemingway in Thursday's attack, including criminal homicide, aggravated assault, burglary and trespassing.

Court records show that Hemingway, who has a criminal history dating back to 2016, was released without bail in July in a February burglary.

title: Charlie Kirk's mother has emotional response to Erika Kirk speculation in rare interview
summary: Kathryn Kirk, the mother of Charlie Kirk, broke her silence, rejecting conspiracy theories about a family rift with Erika Kirk over Charlie Kirk's will and legacy.
story: Erika Kirk, widow of Charlie Kirk, shares a powerful reflection on her grief journey nearly one year after his assassination. In a New York Times essay, she describes the universal nature of loss and details how she manages to find joy with her children while carrying a broken heart, offering a message of hope to others.

In a rare interview, Charlie Kirk's mother pushed back on claims of a family rift with Erika Kirk, saying the loss of her son had brought the two women closer and that Charlie would be upset by the treatment of his wife online.

"We were 100% behind her," Kathryn Kirk told Vanity Fair in a profile of Erika, rejecting claims that Charlie’s parents blame his widow for his death or are fighting with her over his will and Turning Point USA’s future.
"Erika and I have, through the trauma, grown closer," she said. "We knew Charlie in a way that no one else did. We can look at each other’s eyes, and we know the depth of our despair."

Kathryn, who Vanity Fair reported had avoided speaking to journalists until now, said she wants to remain a private citizen. But her silence has become fuel for conspiracy theories about the family’s relationship with Erika.
ERIKA KIRK HITS BACK AT NY TIMES NEWSLETTER ABOUT MARRIAGE AND KIDS, ACCUSES WRITER OF MISSING THE POINT
Charlie Kirk’s parents arrived at a Utah courthouse for a hearing related to the murder case against Tyler Robinson. (Credit: Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
She rejected those claims, according to the outlet, which described her crying as she discussed how upset her son would be over the way his wife has been treated on social media.
ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR
Charlie Kirk’s parents, Robert Kirk and Kathryn Kirk, arrive at Tyler Robinson’s hearing at Fourth District Court in Provo, Utah, July 6, 2026. (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
Kathryn also recalled receiving media inquiries almost immediately after the shooting.
A TMZ reporter "called me even before I talked to my daughter. Before I was running the car," she told Vanity Fair.
The profile also detailed preparations Charlie and Erika were making for their family’s future amid what the magazine described as mounting death threats.

Doug DeGroote, a Turning Point board member who manages the couple’s personal finances, told Vanity Fair they had been working on their will and planned to visit his office to sign the paperwork the Monday after Charlie was killed.
ERIKA KIRK CANCELS UNIVERSITY OF GEORGIA TPUSA EVENT APPEARANCE OVER 'SERIOUS THREATS'

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University Sept. 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking during his American Comeback Tour when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
The night before his death, Charlie had discussed security recommendations with Erika and their pastor, including bulletproof glass shields and vests, according to the outlet.
Turning Point board members, Erika and several close allies also told Vanity Fair that Charlie had made clear he wanted his wife to succeed him if anything happened to him.
INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES
Kathryn said her son had shielded his parents from those conversations "because it would just go right into our fears."
"She knew him more than anyone," a former Turning Point employee told the outlet about Erika’s selection to lead the organization.
ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Erika Kirk, widow of Charlie Kirk and the CEO of Turning Point USA, reacts next to President Donald Trump during a memorial service at State Farm Stadium, in Glendale, Ariz., Sept. 21, 2025. (Reuters/Brian Snyder)
Erika, meanwhile, described the anguish of watching surveillance video of the shooting during a September preliminary hearing.

"Don’t do it. Don’t you dare do it. It’s not too late," she recalled pleading silently as she watched the man on the screen, according to Vanity Fair’s account. She gripped Kathryn’s arm and cried out as the video showed Robinson taking position for the shot.
ERIKA KIRK COMFORTS A STRANGER IN TEARS DURING HEARING FOR HUSBAND'S ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON
Erika Kirk weeps over her late husband Charlie's casket. Turning Point USA CEO Charlie Kirk was killed Sept. 10, 2025, during an event at Utah Valley University. (@MrsErikaKirk/Instagram)
Erika also recalled insisting on seeing her husband’s body at the Utah hospital after a doctor advised against it.
"I looked back at him and said, ‘With all due respect, I want to see what they did to my husband. I didn’t get a kiss goodbye this morning. I just want to kiss my husband,’" she told Vanity Fair.
ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY
Hospital staff removed tubes from Charlie’s mouth, wrapped his neck and cleared away blood before she saw him, the outlet reported.
"I’ll never be able to put it into words," Erika said. "But Charlie had a smirk. It wasn’t sad."

Turning Point USA told Fox News Digital that Erika viewed her selection for Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list as an opportunity to tell her own story and reach an audience less familiar with her, Charlie and the organization.

"Erika believes in being open and engaging with people, including those who come from a very different perspective," a TPUSA representative said. "As Charlie often said, when people stop talking, that’s when bad things happen."
The representative also praised Kathryn’s defense of her daughter-in-law.
"Kathryn Kirk’s words were incredibly powerful. This is a loving, close-knit family that is deeply protective of one another, which is exactly how Charlie was."
