Kreiz will join the company on Oct. 5, indicating that the deal will likely close on that date or shortly after.

“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.

Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount’s streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.

After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department, the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s democratic attorney general Rob Bonta.
For Subscribers
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potential imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.

Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21, which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close Trump ally. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.

After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News, who has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence.
For Subscribers
The merged company pledged it will invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called “ticking fee” kicks in for Paramount Skydance.

In order to build confidence in their merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.

“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the “Block The Merger” coalition, urged that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.

The group criticized the state attorneys general for what they called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld.”
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.

Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.

title: Britain believes Iran was involved in incident near air base used by U.S., prime minister says
summary: There are strong indications that Iran played a part in an incident outside a U.K. airbase that U.S. forces use to strike Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
story: LONDON — There are strong indications Tehran played a part in a security incident outside a British air base that U.S. forces use to facilitate strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.

Burnham said he had chaired an emergency security meeting this week after the incident, which unfolded in the early hours of Sunday. Five men, all British nationals, were arrested on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses and were released on bail earlier this week.
“We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” he said in an interview with Sky News.
”This remains, though, a complex and very serious police investigation, so I can’t say any more at this stage,” he added.
The British Parliament is in recess, but Burnham said he “wouldn’t hesitate” to recall lawmakers “should that be necessary.”
Iran has denied any involvement in the incident.

“The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the Iranian Embassy in Britain said in a statement on X on Monday.
Burnham’s statements were based on intelligence that has been gathered as a result of the investigation into the incident, two senior intelligence officials briefed on the matter told NBC News.
There were two calls that were made early Sunday morning U.K. time that alerted authorities that the five individuals could have been up to something inappropriate, according to one official.
One call to police came from one of the five men in the group at approximately 12:45 am local time, the official said.
British media previously reported this call.

A second call was placed by a local farmer to police around 1:30am local time — a call that was cited by police initially as the reason for the tip on the group’s activities, according to the official.

So far, no charges have been filed against the men, all in their 20s and from London, who were arrested after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London.
Counterterrorism police later took over the case after a major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds.

title: U.S. ends ISIS-fighting mission in Iraq as regional security fears mount
summary: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.
story: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.

Though the Iraqi government welcomed the end of Operation Inherent Resolve, Kurdish officials in the north of the country said they were concerned the Biden-era decision was being carried out even after Iranian missiles pummeled them following the war launched by the United States and Israel earlier this year.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq have attacked U.S. personnel and diplomats, as well as regional allies such as Saudi Arabia. And there are fears Tehran could seek to capitalize on the U.S. withdrawal, with its proxies already celebrating the move, coupled with concerns about a potential resurgence in attacks by the remnants of the Islamic State terrorist group itself.

“We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home,” President Donald Trump said at the White House on Wednesday, adding that the moment was a “victory for the United States” as well as a “decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated, which is the reason we went in there in the first place.”

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “orderly departure” marked “the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” in a statement Wednesday. “This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”

The 2014 U.S.-led mission was successful in dismantling the “caliphate” ISIS governed across around 40% of Iraq and one third of Syria, sweeping through that territory amid instability that followed the U.S. invasion and subsequent withdrawal.
But ISIS has not been defeated entirely in Iraq.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The group comprises “hundreds of fighters” across seven provincial units, according to a United Nations monitoring report in August. This “limited presence” in desert areas generates $500,000 annually through extortion of farmers and shepherds, the report said. But it is “unable to conduct significant attacks” and is only capable of “unsophisticated operations” following the killing and arrest of leaders, it said.

The U.S. expects Iraqi and Kurdish forces to now “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed,” Parnell’s statement said. The Pentagon will “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has been lavished with praise by Trump since entering office in July,  described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase.”

At a handover ceremony in Baghdad, he said this would be “defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”

However, Kurdish officials, who govern the north of Iraq, expressed alarm at the move. The Kurdish Peshmerga Affairs Ministry, which oversees defense, said Monday that the U.S. leaving without establishing any other air defense was “deeply concerning.”
The withdrawal was agreed to under President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, long before the Iran war drastically changed the region’s security landscape.

The Peshmerga Ministry said Monday that 1,000 ballistic missiles have been fired at its territory by Iran since late February. “Some have hit civilian areas, inflicting injuries, material damage and deaths,” it said, nevertheless expressing “sincere gratitude” to the U.S. and its partners “for their cooperation and support.”

The 2003 U.S.-led invasion saw around 150,000 American troops enter the country, toppling leader Saddam Hussein but also triggering a disastrous sectarian war. That combat operation came to an end in 2011, with almost all of the American personnel withdrawn.

The U.S. returned to fight ISIS in 2014, with personnel numbers peaking at almost 9,000 as of 2017. That operation wound down in 2024, and until this week only a small contingent of around 1,500 remained in the Kurdish-governed north.
After this week, a smaller contingent of U.S. forces will stay in Iraq to protect American diplomats.

Iran-backed militant groups have already celebrated the milestone as “a ​historic victory,” as put by Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the powerful umbrella group the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, who described it as “a crushing defeat for the American project.”

And though depleted, ISIS itself “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” according to Col. Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

title: California voters back a billionaire tax, but the proposal falls short of majority support
summary: A new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group shows “yes” supporters leading 48% to 38% on the California ballot measure.
story: A plurality of likely California voters support a proposal on the state’s November ballot that would impose a one-time wealth tax on the richest Californians, but the measure is still short of majority support, according to a new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group poll released Wednesday.
In the poll, 48% said they would vote “yes” on the proposal, while 38% said they would vote “no.” Another 14% said they were undecided.
The 10-point lead for “yes” is outside the poll’s margin of error, which is plus or minus 4 percentage points for each side’s support level.

The spread was almost identical among Hispanic likely voters, according to a companion survey of California: 50% said they’d vote “yes,” 40% said they’d vote “no,” and 10% said they were undecided. Both surveys were conducted Sept. 21-24.

The so-called billionaire tax — which will appear on the November ballot as “Proposition 40” — would implement a one-time 5% tax on the assets of Californians with net worths exceeding $1.1 billion, and it would require the state to spend 90% of the new revenue on healthcare. The remaining 10% would be split between education and food assistance programs.

In addition to the one-time tax on those worth more than $1.1 billion, the measure, if it is passed, would implement a smaller tax on individuals worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

The ballot measure comes amid a growing wealth gap nationwide — and growing ill feeling toward the ultra-wealthy, driving populist campaigning in the 2026 midterm elections. In an earlier national NBC News poll, raising taxes on billionaires was the most popular candidate attribute out of 15 tested

Meanwhile, progressive candidates proposing higher taxes on billionaires have seen success in numerous elections throughout the country, although not all efforts to raise taxes on the wealthy have gone smoothly. In New York City, a judge has pressed pause on Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s bid to tax valuable second homes, citing issues with how Mamdani’s administration implemented the plan.

In California, the billionaire tax proposal on the ballot has divided Democratic leaders. Prominent proponents — including Rep. Ro Khanna, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Tom Steyer, a billionaire activist who unsuccessfully ran for governor — argue it would help close income inequality gaps and help make up for state budget shortfalls as a result of Medicaid cuts in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”

Opponents of the ballot measure, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Democratic candidate to succeed him this year, Xavier Becerra, have argued the initiative would drive wealthy investors and tech leaders from the state.

The details of the proposal, which has been led by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, a large California healthcare workers union, have also sparked opposition from many other unions and Democratic groups. Those groups have taken issue with the fact that other progressive policy priorities, like public education and food assistance, would benefit far less than healthcare from the new revenue.

Many Democratic critics have also joined forces with some Republicans, many of whom have long argued that a wealth tax could destabilize California’s revenue streams by causing the ultrarich to flee the state.
But the new poll showed California voters were largely not worried about the prospect of wealthy California residents’ leaving.

A total of 59% of respondents said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned about that potential outcome, while a total of 41% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about rich people’s leaving the state because of the ballot measure. Among Hispanic voters, 62% said they were either “not” or “not too” concerned, while 38% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned.
For Subscribers
Notably, the poll also found California voters almost evenly split over whether they approve or disapprove of the job performance of Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful.
For Subscribers

Forty-five percent of respondents said they approved of his job performance, while 46% said they disapproved. Another 9% said they weren’t sure. Hispanic voters were more positive about Newsom, with 54% approving and 38% disapproving of his performance as governor.

But when it came to how Democrats felt about a possible Newsom 2028 bid, they overwhelmingly said they’d get behind him. Asked whether they’d be inclined to vote for him if he ran to become the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee in 2028, 66% of Democratic respondents said yes, 15% said no, and 19% said they weren’t sure.

Another November ballot measure, Proposition 39, would, if it is passed, require voters to show a government-issued ID when they cast ballots in person, while mail-in voters would have to provide the last four digits of a designated ID used during registration. Among likely voters, 49% said they would support the measure, while 42% said they would vote against it, and 9% said they were undecided.
Asked about Proposition 39, 55% of Hispanic voters said they would vote “yes” in support of it, while 38% said they would vote “no,” and 7% said they were undecided.

California voters strongly said cost of living and the economy were among the most important issues when they were deciding to vote, with 25% saying “cost of living/inflation” was the most important and 23% saying “economy/jobs.” Another 15% said “immigration and enforcement” was the most important, while 11% said healthcare, and 10% said “foreign policy and the Iran War.” No other issue registered at more than 5%.

Amid the focus on economic issues, a plurality of respondents — 42% — said their “personal financial situation” was “the same” as four years earlier. Thirty-six percent said it was “worse” compared with four years earlier, while 22% said it was “better.”

Meanwhile, most respondents (64%) in reliably blue California overwhelmingly said they disapproved of the job President Donald Trump was doing. Another 31% said they approved, and 5% said they weren’t sure.

Asked how much impact they felt the conflict with Iran was having on the U.S. economy, more than two-thirds (67%) of respondents said it was having a “great” deal of impact. Another 16% said it was having “some” impact, while 7% said “not much,” and 8% said “none.”

title: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to a low-security correctional facility in southern New Jersey, sources said.
story: Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.

This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison

Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.

Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.

“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”

“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.

He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.

Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”

Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem. Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.

Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof. The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.

Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter.
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.

The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.

Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.

Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.

His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July. He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”

title: Judge allows Paramount to close $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros.
story: A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
The seismic merger will bring together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+ and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
Shortly after the judge’s approval, David Ellison, the CEO and controlling shareholder of Paramount Skydance, announced that Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz would become co-CEO of the combined media giant.
Kreiz will join the company on Oct. 5, indicating that the deal will likely close on that date or shortly after.

“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.

Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount’s streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.

After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department, the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s democratic attorney general Rob Bonta.
For Subscribers
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potential imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.

Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21, which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close Trump ally. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.

After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News, who has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence.
For Subscribers
The merged company pledged it will invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called “ticking fee” kicks in for Paramount Skydance.

In order to build confidence in their merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.

“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the “Block The Merger” coalition, urged that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.

The group criticized the state attorneys general for what they called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld.”
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.

Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.

title: Pennsylvania reports 5th measles-related death in the state
summary: Pennsylvania health officials reported on Wednesday the death of an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County who tested positive for measles.
story: Pennsylvania health officials reported on Wednesday the death of an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County who tested positive for measles. It’s the fifth measles-associated death in the state since August.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health didn’t report when the individual died.

The other measles-associated deaths in the state were two infants with measles in Lancaster County, an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County and a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County. The last two happened in mid-September, state health officials reported.
For Subscribers

There have been 943 confirmed cases of measles across 39 counties in Pennsylvania, which is dealing with the largest outbreak of the extremely contagious virus in the U.S. About 176 people have been hospitalized. At least six babies have been born with congenital measles in the state.
For Subscribers

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recognized only two deaths associated with measles this year, although it hasn’t identified in which states they occurred or when. According to the CDC, there have been 3,569 confirmed measles infections nationwide this year.

“We are deeply saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania,” Emily Hilliard, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement, adding that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC director Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection.”

title: Senate Democrats block Sen. Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’
summary: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
story: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster.

The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, sets a federal standard on the issue. It also instructs state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers.

The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He’s facing heat at home from Democratic rival and former senator Sherrod Brown, who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor.

“I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill is merely “optional” for states and won’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans.

“Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.”
Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“I don’t know how you can say something that passed the House of Representatives 417-3 isn’t consequential,” Thune told reporters. “AOC voted for it over there. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.”

An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 points to deal with data centers.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs.
But when asked if the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.”

“I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”

title: U.S. ends ISIS-fighting mission in Iraq as regional security fears mount
summary: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.
story: The last American troops assigned to fight ISIS in Iraq pulled out of the country Wednesday, ending the mission that dismantled the extremists’ self-declared caliphate but raising fears about what might fill the vacuum as the Iran war grinds on.

Though the Iraqi government welcomed the end of Operation Inherent Resolve, Kurdish officials in the north of the country said they were concerned the Biden-era decision was being carried out even after Iranian missiles pummeled them following the war launched by the United States and Israel earlier this year.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq have attacked U.S. personnel and diplomats, as well as regional allies such as Saudi Arabia. And there are fears Tehran could seek to capitalize on the U.S. withdrawal, with its proxies already celebrating the move, coupled with concerns about a potential resurgence in attacks by the remnants of the Islamic State terrorist group itself.

“We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home,” President Donald Trump said at the White House on Wednesday, adding that the moment was a “victory for the United States” as well as a “decisive victory over ISIS, which has been completely decimated, which is the reason we went in there in the first place.”

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “orderly departure” marked “the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq,” in a statement Wednesday. “This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”

The 2014 U.S.-led mission was successful in dismantling the “caliphate” ISIS governed across around 40% of Iraq and one third of Syria, sweeping through that territory amid instability that followed the U.S. invasion and subsequent withdrawal.
But ISIS has not been defeated entirely in Iraq.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The group comprises “hundreds of fighters” across seven provincial units, according to a United Nations monitoring report in August. This “limited presence” in desert areas generates $500,000 annually through extortion of farmers and shepherds, the report said. But it is “unable to conduct significant attacks” and is only capable of “unsophisticated operations” following the killing and arrest of leaders, it said.

The U.S. expects Iraqi and Kurdish forces to now “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed,” Parnell’s statement said. The Pentagon will “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has been lavished with praise by Trump since entering office in July,  described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase.”

At a handover ceremony in Baghdad, he said this would be “defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”

However, Kurdish officials, who govern the north of Iraq, expressed alarm at the move. The Kurdish Peshmerga Affairs Ministry, which oversees defense, said Monday that the U.S. leaving without establishing any other air defense was “deeply concerning.”
The withdrawal was agreed to under President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, long before the Iran war drastically changed the region’s security landscape.

The Peshmerga Ministry said Monday that 1,000 ballistic missiles have been fired at its territory by Iran since late February. “Some have hit civilian areas, inflicting injuries, material damage and deaths,” it said, nevertheless expressing “sincere gratitude” to the U.S. and its partners “for their cooperation and support.”

The 2003 U.S.-led invasion saw around 150,000 American troops enter the country, toppling leader Saddam Hussein but also triggering a disastrous sectarian war. That combat operation came to an end in 2011, with almost all of the American personnel withdrawn.

The U.S. returned to fight ISIS in 2014, with personnel numbers peaking at almost 9,000 as of 2017. That operation wound down in 2024, and until this week only a small contingent of around 1,500 remained in the Kurdish-governed north.
After this week, a smaller contingent of U.S. forces will stay in Iraq to protect American diplomats.

Iran-backed militant groups have already celebrated the milestone as “a ​historic victory,” as put by Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the powerful umbrella group the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, who described it as “a crushing defeat for the American project.”

And though depleted, ISIS itself “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” according to Col. Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

title: For the same ticket on StubHub, different prices for different people
summary: The same seat at Harry Styles’ recent MSG concert could cost $455. Or it could cost $517. The difference comes from the fees that ticket broker StubHub adds.
story: The same seat at an upcoming Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden could cost $455. Or it could cost $517.
The difference comes from the fees that ticket broker StubHub adds. But how much those fees are — and why they can vary — is unclear.

NBC News gathered nine volunteers to check the same StubHub ticket at the same time for Styles’ Oct. 30 concert. They saw eight different prices. The ticket’s base price, set by the seller, was the same for everybody.
The big differences came from the fees StubHub added. One person was charged $72 in fees, while another was charged nearly twice as much, $134.

When the volunteers looked up the same ticket using incognito mode in Google’s Chrome web browser, a private session that doesn’t use cookies, saved logins or site storage, the price discrepancy declined to $19 between the highest- and lowest-priced ticket. When they checked on StubHub’s phone app without being logged in, almost everybody saw the same price, with the exception of just one person who would have been charged $3 more.

The days of a single, transparent price tag are fading. In the digital era, prices can change by the minute, without warning or explanation. Companies can run price experiments, where shoppers are given a range of prices at random to determine the optimal price for profitability. Some companies use surveillance or personalized pricing, where they charge individualized prices based on a customer’s data.

StubHub, one of the largest online ticket resale platforms, has recently faced scrutiny over its business practices, including advertising ticket prices without clearly disclosing mandatory fees, leading to a $10 million Federal Trade Commission settlement, and listing “ghost tickets” from a seller who didn’t actually have them.
The company said it does not use personal information in setting prices but confirmed that ticket prices can vary.

In a statement, StubHub said it “regularly runs randomized tests on pricing — a standard e-commerce practice across retail and marketplace platforms. The fee variations observed in your experiment reflect that testing, not personalization based on individual user data.” The company also said that differences in incognito mode were due to the “natural randomness of a small sample, not a signal that cookie or browsing data drives fee differences.”

Lindsay Owens, author of the new book “Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet,” said price experiments are a way for companies to maximize profit by helping to identify the upper limits of what customers are willing to pay. Even if it is random, it’s still unfair, she said.

“It’s not the resale ticket holder who’s getting that money,” Owens told NBC News. “It’s StubHub, who’s just charging some parents more, some ticket holders more, concertgoers more, just to see their favorite show.”
Owens said it was notable that without access to users’ data trails, the company appeared to have a harder time determining what to charge users.

Mark Tremblay, an economics professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, noted that if the price experiments are random, consumers could take advantage of this by checking multiple ways. “As a consumer, you should shop around on different mediums,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

It’s not just StubHub, Owens said: More and more companies are charging different consumers different prices for the same products. Last year, Owens’ think tank, Groundwork Collaborative, and Consumer Reports found that some Instacart shoppers were shown different prices for the same grocery items. The company said it was price testing and later ended the program.

Companies also have the technology to go a step further, using personal data to determine what a customer is willing to pay and tailor prices to each individual, a practice called surveillance or personalized pricing.

There is no federal ban on personalized pricing, but some states have passed laws regulating the practice. In August, the FTC proposed a policy that would require companies to disclose their use of personalized pricing.

Bob Hedges, a digital fellow at the MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy, said new technology, more powerful algorithms and the explosion of online shopping have made it easier than ever for companies to do this. “Even five years ago, the compute power and real-time processing was not adequate to support some of the real-time pricing algorithms in place today,” he noted.

As companies increasingly use sophisticated algorithms to calculate and change prices in an instant, it’s becoming harder for consumers to know when the price they’re seeing is based on their personal data.
To find out what companies are thinking, Owens said look to their patents. She pointed to DoorDash as an example.

The delivery platform has filed a patent for technology that it says predicts how hungry users are based on things like “a low battery” and “fast scrolling,” suggesting you could be “searching urgently for something to order.”
In a statement, DoorDash said the patent was “never used and has been withdrawn” and was meant to “help people find support if they were struggling on the app.”

The company acknowledged that customers may receive “personalized promotions” for the same order based on “past orders and favorite stores” but said that this practice does not amount to “surveillance pricing.”

title: Britain believes Iran was involved in incident near air base used by U.S., prime minister says
summary: There are strong indications that Iran played a part in an incident outside a U.K. airbase that U.S. forces use to strike Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
story: LONDON — There are strong indications Tehran played a part in a security incident outside a British air base that U.S. forces use to facilitate strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday.

Burnham said he had chaired an emergency security meeting this week after the incident, which unfolded in the early hours of Sunday. Five men, all British nationals, were arrested on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses and were released on bail earlier this week.
“We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” he said in an interview with Sky News.
”This remains, though, a complex and very serious police investigation, so I can’t say any more at this stage,” he added.
The British Parliament is in recess, but Burnham said he “wouldn’t hesitate” to recall lawmakers “should that be necessary.”
Iran has denied any involvement in the incident.

“The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the Iranian Embassy in Britain said in a statement on X on Monday.
Burnham’s statements were based on intelligence that has been gathered as a result of the investigation into the incident, two senior intelligence officials briefed on the matter told NBC News.
There were two calls that were made early Sunday morning U.K. time that alerted authorities that the five individuals could have been up to something inappropriate, according to one official.
One call to police came from one of the five men in the group at approximately 12:45 am local time, the official said.
British media previously reported this call.

A second call was placed by a local farmer to police around 1:30am local time — a call that was cited by police initially as the reason for the tip on the group’s activities, according to the official.

So far, no charges have been filed against the men, all in their 20s and from London, who were arrested after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London.
Counterterrorism police later took over the case after a major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds.

title: Iron deficiency often goes undiagnosed and untreated. New guidelines could change that.
summary: Iron deficiency, which  is often overlooked in girls and younger women. New recommendations for screening could
story: Iron deficiency is often overlooked in girls and younger women, but there are signs that doctors are finally “waking up” to a common blood disorder that can lead to fatigue or difficulty concentrating.
For the first time, the American Society of Hematology is offering guidelines to standardize the diagnosis of iron deficiency.

The new recommendations for screening will “hopefully encourage more proactive treatment for one of the most common blood disorders,” said Dr. Ariela Marshall, an associate professor in the division of hematology, oncology and transplantation at the University of Minnesota.

Almost 40% of teenage girls and young women have low levels of iron, according to a 2023 study published in JAMA, the first research to look at iron deficiency in young women and adolescent girls in the U.S.
Then in 2024, researchers at Brigham and Women’s Hospital found that nearly 1 in 3 of all adults in the U.S. have iron deficiency.

There are indications that the disorder may actually be increasing among adults in the U.S., Leo Buckley, an assistant professor in the internal medicine department at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. Buckley, who was a co-author of the 2024 study, said his team’s most recent research shows a 3% increase in iron deficiency prevalence between 1999 and 2020.

Low levels of iron in the blood are determined through a special blood test that measures ferritin, the protein that stores iron inside our cells. The problem? Normal ranges for ferritin vary from lab to lab, which means some iron deficiencies never get flagged.

The guidelines recommend new “threshold” ferritin levels to indicate low levels of iron in the blood. Based on the markers, some people who were previously believed to have high enough ferritin, or iron stores, would now be considered deficient, said Marshall, who is an expert with the hematological society. The guidelines are also the first to establish threshold levels for women with heavy periods.
Dr. Andrew Eisenberger, director of the classical hematology service at Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, said there’s growing awareness of the condition.
“I actually don’t think that there’s more iron deficiency,” Eisenberger said. “I think we’re just kind of waking up.”
Even before the new guidelines, TikTok influencers turned “ferritin face” into a viral trend, blaming it for a whole range of symptoms — such as pale skin, fatigue, bloating or losing hair.

Women of childbearing age are at the highest risk for iron deficiency, especially those who experience heavy periods, including some perimenopausal women whose periods are heavier because of hormone shifts. Because blood contains iron in red blood cells, losing larger amounts of blood means losing larger amounts of iron every month.
Irritable bowel syndrome, which is more common among women in the U.S., can also cause iron deficiency, said Buckley.
Other health conditions that affect women in greater numbers that can affect iron levels include endometriosis, uterine fibroids, gastric bypass and celiac disease.

Eisenberger said women shouldn’t worry about anecdotal reports of heavier periods linked to Covid vaccines. While studies indicated the mRNA shots caused temporary changes in some women’s menstrual cycles, the cycle changes for a month or two shouldn’t be enough to trigger iron deficiency. “That shouldn’t typically be a permanent reset on the intensity and frequency of someone’s periods,” Eisenberger said.
How iron deficiency is diagnosed
A routine complete blood count lab checks only for hemoglobin to determine anemia, but because the test does not check ferritin levels, a normal result would not rule out iron deficiency.

“Iron is essentially a building block for the red cells, so somebody can be low on iron and not yet have developed anemia,” said Marshall, who said it’s a “big myth” that people with iron deficiency without anemia don’t experience severe symptoms.
Symptoms can range from fatigue to brain fog to a craving for chewing on ice, she said.
Marshall hopes ASH’s guidelines inspire doctors to test the ferritin levels of patients showing signs of low iron to catch iron deficiency earlier.
For Subscribers

“Many of us in hematology realize that iron deficiency is very common, very underdiagnosed and therefore very undertreated,” Marshall said. “It’s an incredibly common condition, and it often has a very simple intervention of giving supplemental iron.”

Typically, a normal level of ferritin in the blood ranges from 12 to 140 nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL) in children ages 6 months to 15 years, from 15 to 205 ng/mL in women, and from 30 to 566 ng/mL in men, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Levels below those ranges would indicate the body doesn’t have enough iron stores, which would suggest an iron deficiency.

Because the new guidelines raise the threshold, or cutoff, number for ferritin, otherwise healthy adults, including menstruating or pregnant women, with ferritin levels at or below 30 ng/mL could now be diagnosed with iron deficiency. For women with heavy periods, the highest risk group, the cutoff level for ferritin is at or below 50 ng/mL.
For Subscribers
The guidelines essentially make it “easier” for someone to be diagnosed with an iron deficiency, Marshall said.
Eisenberger said some women don’t realize they have heavy periods, which is described as bleeding through a tampon or pad every one to two hours.

“I will have a woman come in, and when I ask her about the intensity of her periods, how many days, how many appliances she uses, she’ll say it’s normal and it’s normal for her because it’s normal for what her sister has,” Eisenberger said.
“But I do a double take when she tells me she’s using two pads at once or has to wear a diaper to leave the house and she thinks that’s normal,” he said.
Marshall, who specializes in bleeding and clotting disorders, said the recommendations provide important guidance for doctors who treat women with heavy periods.
“It’s all too common right now that women are told, ‘Oh, your ferritin is 25, but our lab says that it’s not low until it’s less than 15,’” Marshall said.
With the new guidelines, “we can get them treatment, and many of these women will feel significantly better after getting some iron,” she said.
Buckley said iron deficiency symptoms are often downplayed or overlooked by doctors, which delays diagnosis.

“It’s tricky because the symptoms aren’t always obvious,” Buckley said. “It could be something like fatigue. It could be just feeling like your mind is not as sharp if it gets more severe. Some people could have restless leg syndrome or less common side effects.”
Some patients never mention their fatigue to their doctors because they chalk up their tiredness to a busy schedule, Buckley said.
Treating iron deficiency and anemia

If untreated, the condition can progress into iron-deficiency anemia, which happens when the body lacks enough iron to make hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. This type of anemia is rarely life-threatening, but it can affect quality of life.
Symptoms of iron-deficiency anemia include dizziness, shortness of breath, hair loss, headaches and irregular heartbeat. Severe anemia cases can lead to heart issues and pregnancy complications.

Treating iron deficiency or even mild anemia can often be done with oral iron supplements such as ferrous sulfate. “For people who have mild anemia and don’t have chronic constipation or bloating or nausea, I may try putting them on pills first,” Eisenberger said.
Other treatment options include hormonal birth control pills or an IUD to control heavy periods.
Getting iron in your diet
Eating an iron-rich diet helps keep iron stores up.
Pregnant women and those who follow vegetarian or vegan diets need to eat more foods high in iron.
In general, heme iron, which is found in animal products like beef and eggs, is better absorbed than non-heme iron in vegetarian and vegan foods.
Still, those who avoid animal products can supplement with iron or optimize their iron intake by pairing it with foods rich in vitamin C so it’s absorbed better.
“Any doctor who tells a patient that they should not adhere to a vegetarian or vegan diet because of iron deficiency is from the Stone Ages,” Eisenberger said.
Other foods high in iron include:
Leafy greensSeafood, such as tuna or sardinesTofuBeans
Leafy greens
Seafood, such as tuna or sardines
Tofu
Beans
Not everyone has access to nutritious iron-rich foods, said Buckley, who noted that malnutrition is a leading cause of iron deficiency around the world.
“Food insecurity is linked to a lot of other factors that could be causing iron deficiency,” Buckley said.

title: Watchdog finds no criminality in Fed renovation that drew Trump’s scrutiny
summary: The Federal Reserve’s watchdog said it found no grounds to believe federal law was violated in a project that drew criticism from President Donald Trump.
story: WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve’s independent watchdog said Wednesday it found no reasonable grounds to believe there was a violation of federal law in a multibillion-dollar renovation project that drew criticism from President Donald Trump and short-lived scrutiny from federal prosecutors.

But the central bank’s board “had not effectively executed” a contract and its cost-management provisions, according to a 120-page report from the Office of the Inspector General for the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Still, the report “did not identify administrative misconduct” nor any “reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred.”
Later Wednesday, Trump blamed the cost overruns on former Fed chair Jerome Powell, long a target of the president’s ire.

“This is Jerome Powell’s fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.
An attorney for Powell didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The inspector general’s report follows a more than yearlong review into the construction site on the central bank’s Washington, D.C., campus, which became a fixation of the Trump administration as the president also pressured Powell to cut interest rates. Powell, whom Trump nominated for the top Fed job during his first term, remained on the Fed’s board after Kevin Warsh took over as chair in May.

Even after four years of construction and over $2 billion in awarded construction costs, the Fed board had “not established a guaranteed maximum price” for the project, and had set up “insufficient” internal project governance to manage a project of such “magnitude and complexity,” the watchdog said.

Several components of the renovation’s design that drew scrutiny — the building’s marble, water features and a garden terrace — “did not materially contribute to subsequent cost increases,” the watchdog found. The removal of four water features from the renovation plans would not result in significant cost savings, one official told the watchdog, because landscaping and other costs would be needed to replace the fountains.
The watchdog said cost overruns resulted from “inflation, limited subcontractor bidding, substantial Board interior fit-out design changes, and challenging site conditions.”

Moving from a design that focused on closed offices over open workspaces after construction began, the watchdog found, was a “clear example of the consequences of ineffective project management” and “extended the project’s duration and its exposure to inflationary pressures.”

In a letter to Inspector General Michael Horowitz, Warsh wrote that as chairman of the board he agreed about the need to complete the work “in the most efficient and transparent way possible” and said the General Services Administration would be the project executive, effective immediately.
Warsh, who had also been a critic of the renovation, said the American people were owed “a prudent and conscientious use of public funds.”
The GSA is the federal agency tasked with overseeing the federal government’s office buildings, technology services and real estate.
The renovation became a point of contention during a June 25, 2025, Senate hearing. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., asked Powell about the Fed’s renovation project, which caught the White House’s attention.

Scott accused Powell of having “spent billions on lavish renovations” that included “rooftop terraces, custom elevators that open into VIP dining rooms, white marble finishes and even a private art collection.”
Powell denied Scott’s accusations.

“There’s no [VIP] dining room. There’s no new marble. We took down the old marble, we’re putting it back up. We’ll have to use new marble where some of the old marble broke. But there’s no special elevators. There’s just old elevators that have been there. There are no new water features. There’s no beehives, and there’s no roof terrace gardens,” the then-Fed chair said.

On Wednesday, Scott he welcomes the inspector general’s findings. “Inflation does not change the Fed’s responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress,” he wrote in a statement. The Senate Banking Committee, which Scott chairs, “will continue rigorous oversight to ensure the Fed is transparent and stays focused on its mission,” he added.

Shortly after the June hearing, Trump’s Office of Management and Budget director, Russell Vought, wrote Powell a letter saying that the president was “extremely troubled by your management of the Federal Reserve System,” citing the renovation.

“Comparable federal building renovations cost many orders of magnitude less than the office you are building for yourself on the taxpayer’s dime,” Vought added. He later likened the office building renovation to “a palace.”

The Federal Reserve System is not funded by taxpayer money. It is self-funded by the fees it charges on services such as processing checks. It is also funded by the interest it earns on its vast bond portfolio.
Powell denied Vought’s allegations, saying that the central bank had “taken great care to ensure the project is carefully overseen since it was first approved by the Board in 2017.”
As noted by Powell, the project was first approved by the Fed’s entire seven-member Board of Governors. Powell became Fed chair in 2018 after Trump nominated him in late 2017.
The Trump administration did not let up on its campaign against Powell. On July 24, Trump himself made an unprecedented and surprise visit to the Fed’s construction site.

Touring the project alongside Powell and Scott, the president began suggesting that the price tag had ballooned even further. Powell sharply responded, “I haven’t heard that.” Handed a piece of paper by Trump, Powell said that Trump was including a previously completed building project in his new, higher cost estimate.

The Fed also launched a website, which noted that the price tag of the project had risen beyond its first estimate due to changes to the design after voluntarily consulting review boards, and the rising cost of materials, equipment and labor. It also said unforeseen circumstances, such as “more asbestos than anticipated,” contributed.
Still, throughout the year, Trump openly mused about firing Powell, which sometimes rattled markets. A Federal Reserve chair has never been fired before.
After months of more muted complaints about the project, in January a new revelation about it rocked Washington.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In an extraordinary video statement posted to the Fed’s social media pages on a Sunday night in January, Powell announced that “the Department of Justice served the Federal Reserve with grand jury subpoenas.”
He said a criminal probe had been launched against him and the central bank over his earlier Senate testimony.

“No one — certainly not the chair of the Federal Reserve — is above the law,” Powell said. “But this unprecedented action should be seen in the broader context of the administration’s threats and ongoing pressure.” He added: “This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions — or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation.”
Those subpoenas were later blocked by a judge, who said that Trump’s handpicked U.S. attorney in D.C. had “produced essentially zero evidence to suspect Chair Powell of a crime.”

But the damage had already been done. Trump’s U.S. attorney for D.C., Jeanine Pirro — whose aides tried to tour the Fed amid the investigation — said her office closed its probe and referred the matter to the inspector general. The watchdog already had an open inquiry at Powell’s request.

Pirro, a longtime Trump friend, kept her threat to investigate Powell on the table, however. As a result, Powell decided to stay on the Fed board when his term as chair ended on May 22, denying the Trump administration an opportunity to fill an open spot.
Pirro’s office was reviewing the inspector general’s report Wednesday afternoon, a spokesperson said.

The Senate Banking Committee’s top-ranking Democrat, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, applauded the report and said it confirms that “Trump lapdogs U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro and Attorney General Todd Blanche have no basis to restart the President’s witch hunt” against Powell.
“The President should quit trying to fire Fed governors to cover up for his economic failures and instead stop his chaotic tariffs and end his war in Iran,” she said in a statement.
Under Warsh, meanwhile, the Fed has raised rates once and is expected to do so again this year.
Ryan J. Reilly reported from Washington; Steve Kopack from New York.

title: Who Were Thomas Randolph’s 6 Wives in ‘The Widower’ and What Happened to Them?
summary: What happened to Thomas Randoph’s six wives?  Here are all six of his wives and what happened next.
story: The lives of multiple women and their families were irrevocably changed when they ran into Thomas Randolph.

The new Netflix documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios, “The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part,” details the story of a Las Vegas man who has been married six times, and four of his wives have died. The film is directed by Chris Smith, who executive produced the pandemic-era sensation “Tiger King” for Netflix, and begins streaming on Sept. 30.

In 2023, Randolph, now 71, was convicted by a Las Vegas jury for a second time on charges of murdering his sixth wife, Sharon, and a handyman, Mike Miller, whom prosecutors said he double-crossed after hiring Miller to kill his wife.
He had his initial conviction in 2017 overturned by the Nevada Supreme Court in 2020 and then was convicted again after a second trial in 2023.

The new documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios explores a 20-year odyssey involving Randolph, as well as one family’s efforts to bring him to justice. “Dateline” producer and veteran investigative journalist Dan Slepian, who appears in the documentary, was embedded with detectives and frequently interviewed Randolph over the years.
In the documentary, Randolph repeatedly denies any wrongdoing in the deaths of any of his past wives or any involvement in murder-for-hire plots to collect life insurance money.

The film begins with Randolph’s 911 call informing police that his  wife, Sharon, had been shot at their Las Vegas home in 2008. That moment triggers an investigation into Sharon’s death that mushrooms into a deep dive by detectives into Randolph’s chilling past, with Slepian there to film it all.
Here’s what to know about Randolph’s six wives, what happened to each of them, and what connected their experiences with Randolph.
“Eventually, each family came to the conclusion that he was dangerous, horrible, manipulative and ruined their lives,” Slepian tells TODAY.com.

For more on Thomas Randolph and his six marriages, tune into Allegedly, a weekly video podcast on Netflix hosted by NBC News’ Ellison Barber. This week’s episode features a one-on-one conversation with Slepian about his experience following the Randolph case for nearly two decades.
Kathryn Thomas
Married August 1975
Randolph’s first wife, Kathryn, is one of his two former spouses who are still alive.
Now living in Carnation, Washington, she shares in the documentary that many of the chilling behaviors that surfaced in Randolph’s future relationships were evident early.
She said she met Randolph through mutual friends when she was a senior in high school and married him when she was 18 and he was 20. The former couple have two children together.

“He was a very charming and witty person and very intelligent, and I fell for that at first,” she says in the film. “He got really scary, not physically but psychologically. He liked to control you, (and) didn’t want you to have any friends.”
Thomas said she left him when he started seeing other women and doing drugs, recalling that his face “went red” when she told him she had enough.
She also shared two recurrent themes throughout Randolph’s marriages. He had taken out a life insurance policy on her, and he owned several guns.
“He really scared me at that point,” she says.
“You know, there’s always been a lot of insurance on every wife I’ve ever had, and I’ve had a bunch of them,” Randolph says in an audio clip in the documentary.
After she divorced Randolph, she married one of his former friends, a man named Steve Thomas. He says in the film that he was approached by Randolph to see if he would kill someone for money.
“Looking back, I firmly believe she was the target,” Steve Thomas says about his wife.

“This is the first time we know that Tom Randolph tried to groom someone to commit murder,” Dean O’Kelley, the lead detective in the Las Vegas case involving Randolph’s sixth wife, says in the documentary.
Beckie Gault
Married April 1983
Randolph began a relationship with Beckie Gault while he was still with Kathy Thomas. He ended up marrying Gault a day after he divorced his first wife, Slepian says in the documentary.

Rosealie Allred, an aunt of Beckie Gault, says in the film that her niece was getting ready to leave Randolph and move in with Allred when she was found dead in their Utah home in 1986. Investigators ruled it a suicide after finding a gun in her hand and a suicide note, Slepian says in the documentary.

On the night of her death, Randolph was pulled over by police for driving erratically, and a bottle of vodka was found in the vehicle, Slepian says in the documentary. He spent the night in jail and said when he returned home, he found his wife dead in their bed and called 911.
“I’d been in jail for about four hours before my wife killed herself,” Randolph says in audio of a conversation with Slepian in the documentary. “So, I didn’t do this s---.”
O’Kelley, who investigated Randolph’s past after his sixth wife’s death, says in the documentary that Randolph cashed in on insurance policies from Gault’s death worth close to $500,000.

Two years after she died, Randolph was arrested on a charge of first-degree murder after a former handyman, Eric Tarantino, told authorities Randolph tried to hire him to kill Beckie, and he refused, O’Kelley says in the documentary, citing the prosecutors in the case.
Randolph was acquitted by a jury in Utah on the murder charge, which is shown in the film.

He pleaded guilty to felony tampering with a witness for trying to hire a man to kill Tarantino while Randolph was in prison, and the inmate turned out to be an undercover cop, Slepian says in the documentary. He served about 18 months in prison.
Leona Stapleton
Married March 1994
Randolph met his third wife, Leona, in Utah, and then the two moved together to Indiana, Slepian says in the documentary.
They got divorced, and then years later, she died from cancer.
Gayna Allmon
Married October 1995

Barely a year after his previous marriage ended, Randolph married Gayna Almon, who is one of two of Randolph’s ex-wives who is still alive. She says in the documentary that she met him through a personals ad in the newspaper.
“He brought flowers and the next thing I know I’m stupid enough to marry him,” she says.

After Randolph was involved in a shooting at a local bar, police in Edinburgh, Indiana, informed her about the death of Randolph’s second wife, Beckie, Slepian says in the documentary. The police asked if he had taken an insurance policy out on her, and she said he had.
“I had no knowledge of any of that,” she says in the documentary about his past. “I was totally shocked.”

One night, a bullet went through the floor right near where she was sitting while Randolph said he was cleaning his firearms, O’Kelley says in the documentary. She says she waited until he went to work and then left him for good.

A former associate of Randolph’s named Glenn Morrison appears in the film and says Randolph offered him to make “some quick money” by shooting Allmon and making it look like a robbery. Morrison said he declined.
Randolph denies repeatedly in the documentary that he ever asked anyone to commit a murder-for-hire.
No investigation was ever done, and Randolph was never charged with any crimes in connection to his fourth wife.
Frances Randolph
Married August 1997
Randolph met his fifth wife while he was still with his fourth wife, and then convinced Frances to leave her husband to marry him, Slepian says in the documentary.

Carolyn Austin, the sister of Frances Randolph, says in the film that Frances had a heart condition that needed to be addressed before she was older, and Randolph encouraged her to get the procedure done.
She went to a doctor who was selected by Randolph, according to Austin. While recovering from surgery, Frances took a turn for the worse and died, O’Kelley says in the documentary.
Her death was never declared a murder, and Randolph insists to this day it was due to medical malpractice, Slepian says in the film.
Randolph collected money from life insurance policies on Frances and also received a settlement from a wrongful death lawsuit against the hospital, according to Slepian.

In a chilling aftermath, Austin found a VHS video that Randolph had his late wife make, which she shows in the documentary. The tape serves as a video will in which Frances declares her wishes to have Randolph inherit everything from her.
“I’m making this tape so people will know what I want when I pass away,” Frances says in the video.
“One of the moments that stand out the most to me is the video will that we saw on that VHS tape,” Slepian tells TODAY.com. “You can hear him coaching her.”
Sharon Causse
Married March 2007
Randolph moved from Utah to Las Vegas when he married Sharon Causse 10 years after his previous marriage.
Three months into their marriage, Causse made a will leaving almost everything to Randolph, and he took out three life insurance policies for about $350,000, Slepian says in the documentary.

The two were married for barely more than a year when Randolph called 911 in May 2008 to report that his wife had been shot by an intruder. Randolph said he shot and killed the man in self defense, according to audio of the 911 call in the documentary.
The alleged intruder was a man Randolph knew named Mike Miller, who had worked for him as a handyman, which he tells the 911 operator.
Prosecutors declined to charge Randolph with any crime at the time.

Causse’s daughter, Colleen Beyer, describes in the film that she was fearful of Randolph after she informed him that he would not be inheriting Sharon’s possessions after Beyer was named the administrator of her mother’s will. When she had the locks changed on her home, Randolph showed up to confront her but was stopped at the door by O’Kelley, according to footage in the documentary.

Eight months after his sixth wife’s death, Randolph was charged with two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder in the deaths of his wife and Miller. However, it took 8½ years for him to stand trial, as he is shown in the film repeatedly hiring new lawyers to delay the case.
A jury initially convicted him in 2017 on two counts of murder with a deadly weapon and a count of conspiracy to commit murder, and he was sentenced to the death penalty.

However, the Nevada Supreme Court overturned the guilty verdict in 2020. The court ruled that the jury should not have been allowed to hear “prior-bad-act evidence” about Randolph’s previous trial in 1988 on the murder charge involving the death of his wife Beckie, according to NBC affiliate KSNV.

After winning his appeal, Randolph faced another trial in Clark County, Nevada, in 2023 and was convicted a second time by a jury on charges of murder and conspiracy to commit murder. His most recent appeal was denied by the Nevada Supreme Court in September 2026.

Beyer testified at both Las Vegas trials in the hopes of seeing justice for her mother. The ordeal lasted so long that her daughter, who she was pregnant with when Slepian began filming with her, was 15 years old by the time Randolph was convicted by a jury for the second time.

title: Craig Melvin Is Nominated In People’s Sexiest Man Alive Poll. How to Vote
summary: Craig Melvin is nominated in the “hotter than your cup of coffee in the morning” category in People’s Sexiest Man Alive Readers’ Choice Poll.
story: People’s Sexiest Man Alive Readers’ Choice poll is back, and TODAY’s very own Craig Melvin is among the contenders.

The co-anchor is among the nominees featured in the “hotter than your cup of coffee in the morning” category for morning show personalities, going up against Michael Strahan, Gio Benitez and Vladimir Duthiers.
The TODAY team celebrated the news Sept. 30 with cups of coffee.
“Am I being punk’d right now?” Craig said of his nomination.
“Let’s vote!” Jenna Bush Hager said.
“Vote early and often,” Savannah Guthrie chimed in.
“Try to stuff the ballot,” Carson Daly said.
Voting in the survey runs through Oct. 12. The results will be available starting Oct. 20. Readers can vote in the poll here.
Other Readers’ Choice poll categories for 2026 include “sexiest fake hockey player,” “sexiest cat dad” and “sexiest period drama dreamboat.”

This isn’t the first time Craig has appeared in the magazine’s Readers’ Choice poll. In 2023, he was nominated for sexiest morning show host. That same year, Al Roker was also up for sexiest grandpa. Mark Consuelos ultimately took home the morning show host award, while Pierce Brosnan won sexiest grandpa.

title: Where Is Thomas Randolph from ‘The Widower’ Now?
summary: Where is Thomas Randolph from The Widower now? What did he do? Where is he serving time?
story: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.
Out of Thomas Randolph’s six marriages, four of his wives are dead — three of them under mysterious circumstances.

The new Netflix documentary from Library Films and NBC News Studios, “The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part,” chronicles the investigation into Randolph as it unfolded in real time through the lens of veteran Dateline producer and investigative journalist Dan Slepian, who was embedded with detectives. The story includes chilling background on his early marriages, stunning legal twists, and the push for justice by those left in the wreckage of his wake.

Randolph also shares his side of everything in the documentary through interviews with veteran “Dateline” producer and investigative journalist Dan Slepian, who has followed all the twists and turns of Randolph’s story for 18 years.
